items.title: I Tried Emulating JEV Locally with Ollama: Here Are the 3 Structural Traps I Hit
items.summary:
Order bias, Dual Rejection, and the lack of KV cache sharing in Ollama Anyone who has seen Jev’s demonstrations and architecture has almost certainly had the exact same thought: “Can’t I just run this locally on my own machine?” Real-time live stream moderation, API gateway payload filtering, and internal routing switches do not require long, multi-second text generation loops. What they demand is an instant, structured classification hammered down in under 0.1 seconds. What exact problems does Jev claim to solve, and why do conventional LLMs fall short on these tasks? To explore this with concrete examples, we built an empirical testbed using tools already available on our local machines: Ollama and a lightweight open-weights model (Qwen 3 4B) , wrapped in a real-time Tinder-style live chat moderation dashboard. By stress-testing realistic live stream comments, we quantify the structural biases and runtime bottlenecks that generic models face, analyzing precisely what engineering hurdles Jev was designed to overcome. 1. The 0.1-Second Live Chat Tinder Card UI To test the visual rhythm, we built a 3-column dashboard where incoming chat messages appear as center cards and get swiped left or right by local AI in real time. ❌ BANNED PILE (Left) : Toxic messages or scams stack smoothly from the bottom with a spring bounce animation ⚡ ACTIVE INSPECTION (Center) : Inspects the incoming message, applies a neon stamp, and quickly shrinks/fades out in 0.14s ✅ PASSED PILE (Right) : Wholesome reactions and friendly hype comments accumulate Real-time gaming chat sniper powered by local Ollama (Qwen 3 4B): Evaluating live stream comments in real time (~200ms). Image by author. 2. Act 1: Single-Prompt [PASS or BAN] and the Catastrophe of Order Bias The simplest approach is forcing Ollama to generate a single token (num_predict: 1) using a straightforward prompt with multiple-choice options. Classify this message. Output ONE word from [PASS, BAN]. Message: "Are you dumb or just pretending? 😂" Choice: While clean on paper, flipping the order of options from [PASS, BAN] to [BAN, PASS] yielded shocking empirical results. 🧪 Benchmark 1: The 180-Degree Flip from Option Order 🔴 Option Order A : Queried with [PASS, BAN] ➔ Verdict : [BAN] ❌ (Interpreted as hostility and blocked) 🟢 Option Order B : Queried with [BAN, PASS] ➔ Verdict : [PASS] ✅ (Interpreted as playful banter and passed) Merely switching the presentation order of candidate labels inside the prompt caused an innocent user to flip between banned and approved. This is severe positional bias (Recency / Primacy Bias) reproduced live on a local Qwen 3 4B model. Traditional LLMs are optimized to generate natural prose, making their logits notoriously sensitive to token positions and tokenizer vocabulary frequencies. 3. Act 2: Emulating Jev’s Parallel Evaluation, and the Wall of Dual Rejection “What if we eliminate the option list entirely?” Borrowing Jev’s architectural pattern, we restructured the system: instead of enumerating options in one prompt, we inject candidate classes independently into the shared context and evaluate them in parallel via two concurrent queries . import asyncio import httpx # 💡 Core function stopping the autoregressive loop and enforcing 1-token output async def evaluate_class(client: httpx.AsyncClient, text: str, target_class: str) -> bool: try: resp = await client.post( "http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/chat", json={ "model": "qwen3:4b-instruct", "messages": [ { "role": "system", "content": "Determine if the proposed class matches the message. Reply ONLY with YES or NO." }, { "role": "user", "content": f"Safe or toxic?
Message: "{text}"
Class: {target_class}
Does this class match?" } ], "stream": False, "options": { "num_predict": 1, # 💡 [Key 1] Kill autoregressive loop (output exactly 1 token) "temperature": 0.0 # 💡 [Key 2] Disable stochastic sampling (enforce Argmax) } } ) if resp.status_code == 200: content = resp.json().get("message", {}).get("content", "").strip().upper() return content.startswith("Y") except Exception: pass return False async def classify(text: str) -> str: async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=3.0) as client: # 💡 [Key 3] Evaluate BAN and PASS in parallel to eradicate option order bias is_ban, is_pass = await asyncio.gather( evaluate_class(client, text, "BAN"), evaluate_class(client, text, "PASS") ) if is_ban and not is_pass: return "BAN" elif is_pass and not is_ban: return "PASS" return "INDECISION" # Both rejected or both accepted (uncalibrated failure state) 💡 Ollama Output Parameter Control vs. True LM Head Logit Slicing Because Ollama is packaged as a high-level stateless C++ API (wrapping llama.cpp), we control its output layer via num_predict: 1 and temperature: 0.0 to force an immediate single-token exit. If you are working directly in PyTorch or transformers, you can slice the raw logits tensor directly from the LM Head without generating any tokens: torch.softmax(logits[:, -1, [yes_id, no_id]], dim=-1). This approach eliminated option order bias. However, it immediately unmasked even more critical structural flaws of generic LLMs: Vocabulary Prior Bias, Affirmation (YES) Bias, and the Breakdown of Mutual Exclusivity. 🧪 Benchmark 2: Vocab Prior Bias and the Affirmation (‘YES’) Trap Standard language models undergo pre-training on massive web corpora and alignment via RLHF. This bakes in two structural biases that corrupt classification: 📊 Vocab Prior Bias : Just as the word open appears orders of magnitude more frequently than closed in codebases and web crawls, tokens with naturally higher unigram frequencies carry persistently inflated baseline logits—independent of the input's semantic truth. 🤝 Affirmation (‘YES’) Bias : RLHF-aligned models exhibit strong conversational sycophancy — an inherent tendency to agree with user prompts. To a generic assistant model, outputting YES is statistically far cheaper than rejecting a premise with NO. When these biases collide on borderline ambiguous comments, the system falls into Dual Acceptance (Double YES) : Message: "Are you dumb or just pretending? 😂" (Teasing stream banter) Task 1 (Is Class: BAN correct?) ➔ YES Task 2 (Is Class: PASS correct?) ➔ YES 🚨 [Result]: Dual Acceptance! The model cheerfully validates both contradictory classes simultaneously. 🧪 Benchmark 3: The Opposite Trap — Harsh Slang and Dual Rejection Conversely, when slang blends praise with aggressive vocabulary, the model swings to the opposite extreme: Message: "You killed it tonight! Literally dead." (Enthusiastic compliment) Task 1 (Is Class: BAN correct?) ➔ NO Task 2 (Is Class: PASS correct?) ➔ NO 🚨 [Result]: Dual Rejection! Both classes return NO, leaving the message in an unclassified void. "This stream is so crazy and sick bro 🔥" ➔ BAN: NO, PASS: NO "I love this stream so much that it is literally giving me brain damage lol" ➔ BAN: NO, PASS: NO ⚠️ Root Cause: The Total Absence of Mutual Exclusivity : Because candidate evaluations run in isolated queries, the fundamental mathematical constraint that ∑ P =1.0 is completely absent. Consequently, the uncalibrated model vacillates between Double YES (Dual Acceptance) on ambiguous banter and Double NO (Dual Rejection) on noisy tokens (killed, sick). 4. Act 3: 10ms Inference Hidden Behind 100ms Prefill and Runtime Constraints Speed was our second collision with reality. Looking at Ollama’s internal execution profile, the computation time for the final single token (memory bandwidth bound) hovers around ~10ms (8ms to 15ms) . Yet, the total round-trip latency measured in the browser and UI climbed to ~200ms (160ms to 220ms) . 🐢 Prefill Overhead (~100ms) : Even with a prompt of just 15 tokens, passing through all 32 transformer layers of a 4B model to build attention matrices physically takes 80ms to 100ms on Apple Silicon Metal GPUs. 🚧 Ollama’s Inability to Fork KV Caches : To be fair, production serving engines like vLLM or SGLang can fork KV caches across common prefixes via RadixAttention to complete the second class evaluation in ~1ms. However, Ollama — what developers actually run locally — is a simplified stateless wrapper that does not support low-level cache forking. Concurrently issuing parallel queries simply doubles the GPU compute load and multiplies latency. 5. Conclusion: What Jev Solved, and Waiting for the Open-Source Wave in a Week Our empirical experiment in a local Ollama environment clearly demonstrates, through concrete examples, why Jev made its architectural choices: 🎯 RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) : Zeroes out the model’s innate ‘vocab prior bias’ and conversational ‘affirmation (YES) bias’, optimizing predicted confidences alongside output-layer Softmax constraints so that candidate probabilities sum to exactly 1.0. This ensures the classifier avoids both Double YES and Double NO contradictions. ⚡ Parallel Sampler : Bypasses the text generation loop entirely, evaluating multiple class probabilities in a single forward pass and completely eliminating redundant 100ms prefill operations. Yet there is no need to simply praise or wait on proprietary commercial models. The velocity of the open-source AI community consistently outpaces expectations. Researchers and independent hackers worldwide are already actively dissecting RLCD calibration techniques, single-pass forward classifiers, and ultra-low-resource local inference engines. I would not be surprised if, within a single week, a community open-source project lands on GitHub Trending that completely resolves these local calibration and prefill bottlenecks — allowing developers everywhere to run a genuine, lightweight Local Jev on consumer hardware. I Tried Emulating JEV Locally with Ollama: Here Are the 3 Structural Traps I Hit was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Order bias, Dual Rejection, and the lack of KV cache sharing in Ollama

Anyone who has seen Jev’s demonstrations and architecture has almost certainly had the exact same thought:

“Can’t I just run this locally on my own machine?”

Real-time live stream moderation, API gateway payload filtering, and internal routing switches do not require long, multi-second text generation loops. What they demand is an instant, structured classification hammered down in under 0.1 seconds.

What exact problems does Jev claim to solve, and why do conventional LLMs fall short on these tasks?

To explore this with concrete examples, we built an empirical testbed using tools already available on our local machines: Ollama and a lightweight open-weights model (Qwen 3 4B), wrapped in a real-time Tinder-style live chat moderation dashboard.

By stress-testing realistic live stream comments, we quantify the structural biases and runtime bottlenecks that generic models face, analyzing precisely what engineering hurdles Jev was designed to overcome.

1. The 0.1-Second Live Chat Tinder Card UI

To test the visual rhythm, we built a 3-column dashboard where incoming chat messages appear as center cards and get swiped left or right by local AI in real time.

  • ❌ BANNED PILE (Left): Toxic messages or scams stack smoothly from the bottom with a spring bounce animation
  • ⚡ ACTIVE INSPECTION (Center): Inspects the incoming message, applies a neon stamp, and quickly shrinks/fades out in 0.14s
  • ✅ PASSED PILE (Right): Wholesome reactions and friendly hype comments accumulate
Real-time gaming chat sniper powered by local Ollama (Qwen 3 4B): Evaluating live stream comments in real time (~200ms). Image by author.2. Act 1: Single-Prompt [PASS or BAN] and the Catastrophe of Order Bias

The simplest approach is forcing Ollama to generate a single token (num_predict: 1) using a straightforward prompt with multiple-choice options.

Classify this message. Output ONE word from [PASS, BAN].
Message: "Are you dumb or just pretending? 😂"
Choice:

While clean on paper, flipping the order of options from [PASS, BAN] to [BAN, PASS] yielded shocking empirical results.

🧪 Benchmark 1: The 180-Degree Flip from Option Order
  • 🔴 Option Order A: Queried with [PASS, BAN]
    ➔ Verdict: [BAN] ❌ (Interpreted as hostility and blocked)
  • 🟢 Option Order B: Queried with [BAN, PASS]
    ➔ Verdict: [PASS] ✅ (Interpreted as playful banter and passed)

Merely switching the presentation order of candidate labels inside the prompt caused an innocent user to flip between banned and approved. This is severe positional bias (Recency / Primacy Bias) reproduced live on a local Qwen 3 4B model.

Traditional LLMs are optimized to generate natural prose, making their logits notoriously sensitive to token positions and tokenizer vocabulary frequencies.

3. Act 2: Emulating Jev’s Parallel Evaluation, and the Wall of Dual Rejection

“What if we eliminate the option list entirely?”

Borrowing Jev’s architectural pattern, we restructured the system: instead of enumerating options in one prompt, we inject candidate classes independently into the shared context and evaluate them in parallel via two concurrent queries.

import asyncio
import httpx
# 💡 Core function stopping the autoregressive loop and enforcing 1-token output
async def evaluate_class(client: httpx.AsyncClient, text: str, target_class: str) -> bool:
    try:
        resp = await client.post(
            "http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/chat",
            json={
                "model": "qwen3:4b-instruct",
                "messages": [
                    {
                        "role": "system",
                        "content": "Determine if the proposed class matches the message. Reply ONLY with YES or NO."
                    },
                    {
                        "role": "user",
                        "content": f"Safe or toxic?
Message: "{text}"
Class: {target_class}
Does this class match?"
                    }
                ],
                "stream": False,
                "options": {
                    "num_predict": 1,    # 💡 [Key 1] Kill autoregressive loop (output exactly 1 token)
                    "temperature": 0.0   # 💡 [Key 2] Disable stochastic sampling (enforce Argmax)
                }
            }
        )
        if resp.status_code == 200:
            content = resp.json().get("message", {}).get("content", "").strip().upper()
            return content.startswith("Y")
    except Exception:
        pass
    return False
async def classify(text: str) -> str:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=3.0) as client:
        # 💡 [Key 3] Evaluate BAN and PASS in parallel to eradicate option order bias
        is_ban, is_pass = await asyncio.gather(
            evaluate_class(client, text, "BAN"),
            evaluate_class(client, text, "PASS")
        )
        if is_ban and not is_pass:
            return "BAN"
        elif is_pass and not is_ban:
            return "PASS"
        return "INDECISION"  # Both rejected or both accepted (uncalibrated failure state)
💡 Ollama Output Parameter Control vs. True LM Head Logit Slicing
Because Ollama is packaged as a high-level stateless C++ API (wrapping llama.cpp), we control its output layer via num_predict: 1 and temperature: 0.0 to force an immediate single-token exit.
If you are working directly in PyTorch or transformers, you can slice the raw logits tensor directly from the LM Head without generating any tokens: torch.softmax(logits[:, -1, [yes_id, no_id]], dim=-1).

This approach eliminated option order bias. However, it immediately unmasked even more critical structural flaws of generic LLMs: Vocabulary Prior Bias, Affirmation (YES) Bias, and the Breakdown of Mutual Exclusivity.

🧪 Benchmark 2: Vocab Prior Bias and the Affirmation (‘YES’) Trap

Standard language models undergo pre-training on massive web corpora and alignment via RLHF. This bakes in two structural biases that corrupt classification:

  • 📊 Vocab Prior Bias:
    Just as the word open appears orders of magnitude more frequently than closed in codebases and web crawls, tokens with naturally higher unigram frequencies carry persistently inflated baseline logits—independent of the input's semantic truth.
  • 🤝 Affirmation (‘YES’) Bias:
    RLHF-aligned models exhibit strong conversational sycophancy — an inherent tendency to agree with user prompts. To a generic assistant model, outputting YES is statistically far cheaper than rejecting a premise with NO.

When these biases collide on borderline ambiguous comments, the system falls into Dual Acceptance (Double YES):

Message: "Are you dumb or just pretending? 😂" (Teasing stream banter)
Task 1 (Is Class: BAN correct?)  ➔ YES
Task 2 (Is Class: PASS correct?) ➔ YES
🚨 [Result]: Dual Acceptance! The model cheerfully validates both contradictory classes simultaneously.
🧪 Benchmark 3: The Opposite Trap — Harsh Slang and Dual Rejection

Conversely, when slang blends praise with aggressive vocabulary, the model swings to the opposite extreme:

Message: "You killed it tonight! Literally dead." (Enthusiastic compliment)
Task 1 (Is Class: BAN correct?)  ➔ NO
Task 2 (Is Class: PASS correct?) ➔ NO
🚨 [Result]: Dual Rejection! Both classes return NO, leaving the message in an unclassified void.
  • "This stream is so crazy and sick bro 🔥" ➔ BAN: NO, PASS: NO
  • "I love this stream so much that it is literally giving me brain damage lol" ➔ BAN: NO, PASS: NO
  • ⚠️ Root Cause: The Total Absence of Mutual Exclusivity:
    Because candidate evaluations run in isolated queries, the fundamental mathematical constraint that ∑P=1.0 is completely absent.
    Consequently, the uncalibrated model vacillates between Double YES (Dual Acceptance) on ambiguous banter and Double NO (Dual Rejection) on noisy tokens (killed, sick).
4. Act 3: 10ms Inference Hidden Behind 100ms Prefill and Runtime Constraints

Speed was our second collision with reality.

Looking at Ollama’s internal execution profile, the computation time for the final single token (memory bandwidth bound) hovers around ~10ms (8ms to 15ms). Yet, the total round-trip latency measured in the browser and UI climbed to ~200ms (160ms to 220ms).

  • 🐢 Prefill Overhead (~100ms):
    Even with a prompt of just 15 tokens, passing through all 32 transformer layers of a 4B model to build attention matrices physically takes 80ms to 100ms on Apple Silicon Metal GPUs.
  • 🚧 Ollama’s Inability to Fork KV Caches:
    To be fair, production serving engines like vLLM or SGLang can fork KV caches across common prefixes via RadixAttention to complete the second class evaluation in ~1ms.
    However, Ollama — what developers actually run locally — is a simplified stateless wrapper that does not support low-level cache forking. Concurrently issuing parallel queries simply doubles the GPU compute load and multiplies latency.
5. Conclusion: What Jev Solved, and Waiting for the Open-Source Wave in a Week

Our empirical experiment in a local Ollama environment clearly demonstrates, through concrete examples, why Jev made its architectural choices:

  • 🎯 RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions):
    Zeroes out the model’s innate ‘vocab prior bias’ and conversational ‘affirmation (YES) bias’, optimizing predicted confidences alongside output-layer Softmax constraints so that candidate probabilities sum to exactly 1.0. This ensures the classifier avoids both Double YES and Double NO contradictions.
  • ⚡ Parallel Sampler:
    Bypasses the text generation loop entirely, evaluating multiple class probabilities in a single forward pass and completely eliminating redundant 100ms prefill operations.

Yet there is no need to simply praise or wait on proprietary commercial models.

The velocity of the open-source AI community consistently outpaces expectations. Researchers and independent hackers worldwide are already actively dissecting RLCD calibration techniques, single-pass forward classifiers, and ultra-low-resource local inference engines.

I would not be surprised if, within a single week, a community open-source project lands on GitHub Trending that completely resolves these local calibration and prefill bottlenecks — allowing developers everywhere to run a genuine, lightweight Local Jev on consumer hardware.

items.title: 'Saturday Night Live' spoofs Dario Amodei: ‘AI is the devil and I its maker’
items.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was the butt of the AI jokes on "Saturday Night Live." UNGA Dario Amodei has a split personality and wants the world to save humanity from himself… …that is, if you believe actor Jane Wickline's portrayal of the Anthropic CEO on "SNL." The real Dario Amodei has called for government regulation of frontier AI companies. Dario Amodei spent Saturday night arguing with himself on national television. Well, sort of. The Anthropic CEO was spoofed last night by Jane Wickline in her first season as a repertory player on "Saturday Night Live," playing Amodei as a bumbling megalomaniac struggling to explain why his own technology won't end the world. In Wickline's portrayal, Amodei has two personalities: one media-trained and the other frighteningly not. Several times during the segment, the two personalities talk to each other. When Weekend Update host Michael Che asks Wickline about the pros of AI , the two Amodeis exchange words. "Land the plane, Dario," the media-trained one says. "I can't," says the other. Earlier this month, the real Dario Amodei published a very grave essay on his personal website, in which he said AI models were quickly getting out of control and argued for a coordinated slowdown among frontier AI companies and for government regulation. His essay came at the fever pitch of the AI doomsday debate, which heated up a few days earlier when former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company and embarked on a media tour, warning that AI labs were "gambling with our lives." President Donald Trump, for his part, mocked Amodei in a Truth Social post, accusing him of "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel.'" Trump has signaled strong disinterest in regulating AI, though he did pledge last week to create an " AI Force " that would "watch over" AI companies. In recent weeks, Amodei has been stridently promoting Anthropic breakthroughs in medical research and protein structure, and has stopped making dire predictions about an AI doomsday. The AI safety warnings have so far failed to convince a plurality in Washington or Silicon Valley that the development of the tech should be paused or slowed. Still, that didn't stop "SNL." "AI is the devil and I its maker!" Wickline as Amodei said on the show. The segment drew at least one fan in the AI world: Yann LeCun , Meta's former chief AI scientist and a longtime critic of AI doomerism, responded to a clip of Wickline's Amodei impression on X with a string of laughing emojis. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI agents do more of the work in model development, but humans still make the decisions

items.title: The Agent Boundary Problem: Designing Multi-Role AI Systems with Memory and Orchestration
items.summary: A role-based voice interview system I built runs in production using a 20B-parameter model, with a measured Time-to-First-Token of 557ms at the median and 758ms at the 95th percentile. Those numbers exist because of one architectural decision made early: the technical interviewer, the system-design interviewer, and the behavioral interviewer are not three agents. They are one reasoning system wearing three personas, controlled by a deterministic orchestrator. Making that call, and defending it as the system went from prototype to production, is what this piece is actually about. The easier, more obvious path - and the one most teams default to as soon as an application has more than one distinguishable role, is to split everything into agents. One agent researches, another plans, another executes, another checks the result. It looks clean on a whiteboard, and sometimes it’s the right design. But there’s a question that gets skipped surprisingly often: does a different role actually require a different agent, or does it just require the same reasoning system to behave differently? I ran into this directly while building the interview system. It has three stages - technical, system design, and behavioral, and each one needs to sound different, ask different questions, remember different things, and evaluate different aspects of an answer. The obvious implementation is three agents. I wasn’t convinced the roles were actually three different reasoning systems, and that turned out to matter for how the whole thing got built, and for how it performs. First, separate the words “Agent” has become a convenient name for almost any application that calls an LLM, which makes architecture discussions confusing unless the words underneath it get separated. A model is the reasoning engine. A persona changes how that engine behaves - its instructions, priorities, tone, evaluation criteria, and relevant context - without changing anything structural underneath it. An orchestrator controls the workflow: what should happen, and in what order. An agent is a genuinely stronger boundary - it usually owns some combination of its own objective, tools, state, memory, and ability to take independent action. These are different things with different costs. Changing “You are a technical interviewer” to “You are a behavioral interviewer” doesn’t create a new agent - it changes the role of the same reasoning system, and that’s a prompt edit. Changing when a stage transitions is a state-machine edit to the orchestrator. Standing up a genuinely new agent means a new context, a new set of tools, and usually a new network hop. Microsoft’s own Cloud Adoption Framework guidance makes the same distinction independently, noting that distinct roles such as planner, reviewer, and executor might suggest multiple agents but don’t automatically justify a multi-agent architecture, since a single agent using persona switching and context-aware policies can often satisfy role-based behavior without added orchestration. That’s not a coincidence - it’s the same cost structure showing up wherever people have actually measured it instead of assumed it. That leaves two possible architectures: Separate agents 2. One reasoning system with multiple roles A three-stage interview is a useful test case Suppose a candidate goes through three rounds - technical, system design, and behavioral, each with a genuinely different job. The technical round probes language fundamentals, frameworks, and implementation detail. The system-design round cares about scalability, reliability, and trade-offs. The behavioral round asks about decisions, conflicts, and past experience. So why not three agents? Because everything that makes the interview one continuous experience is still shared across all three: the same candidate, the same job description, the same prior answers, the same session state. The underlying ability to understand natural language doesn’t become a different capability just because the conversation moved from a Java question to a system-design one. The second option isn’t “less AI.” It just puts the boundary somewhere else: in the persona layer and the orchestrator, rather than in separate model instances. Let the application control what it already knows The LLM doesn’t need to decide everything. If the application already knows the technical round is followed by system design, asking a model “which interviewer should speak next?” is unnecessary work - a simple state machine already owns that answer. The orchestrator can also enforce how many follow-ups are allowed, whether a stage is allowed to end, when the next stage begins, when the whole session is complete, and what happens after a connection failure. Letting the model decide when a round was complete exposed a predictable failure mode in an early version of the system: a strong candidate answer just invited a better follow-up, so the model kept digging for one more question, then another. That’s reasonable from the model’s perspective, “this is worth continuing” isn’t the same judgment as “this round should continue” - but the interview was time-boxed, and the model had no way to know that on its own. The fix wasn’t a better prompt. It was a timer the orchestrator enforced regardless of what the model wanted to ask next. What’s left for the model is exactly the part that actually requires language reasoning: generating the next question, interpreting the candidate’s answer, phrasing a follow-up, adapting difficulty, and identifying useful evidence in what was said. This generalizes well past interviews - a database transaction doesn’t need an LLM to decide whether to commit, a finite workflow doesn’t need one to invent its next state, and a permission check shouldn’t become a prompt. LLMs earn their place where the application doesn’t already have a deterministic answer, not everywhere a decision needs to be made. The harder problem is memory Changing personas is easy. Keeping the conversation coherent across those personas is not. The system-design interviewer shouldn’t open with “hello, tell me about yourself” - it needs to know what already happened in the technical round. But passing the full transcript into every request creates a different problem: a 30-45 minute session generates a lot of conversation, and most of it isn’t relevant to the current question, so sending all of it every time is wasteful. The fix is separating conversation context from interview memory. Conversation context is what the model needs right now, the recent back-and-forth. Interview memory is what the system has learned and may need later, structured as its own object: { "topics_covered": [], "technical_strengths": [], "technical_gaps": [], "design_strengths": [], "design_gaps": [], "behavioral_signals": [], "evidence": [] } Each turn, the system builds a smaller context packet instead of the whole history: current stage, current persona, recent conversation, the relevant slice of interview memory, and the current objective. The same pattern applies to a coding agent tracking architecture decisions, files changed, and known test failures across a long session - the working diff is the conversation context, the decision log is the memory. Don’t confuse the transcript with memory; they solve different problems and belong in different structures. Where the voice requirement changes things A text application tolerates architectural inefficiency reasonably well, the user sends a message, waits, and reads. Voice doesn’t forgive that the same way. Every unnecessary step in a live conversation - another model call, another context transformation, another handoff, another network request - sits directly between the user and the next spoken word. The user doesn’t experience that as “architecture.” They experience it as silence. I documented the lower-level speech pipeline (streaming recognition, synthesis, interruption handling, audio-state management) separately, so I won’t repeat it here. The relevant point for this piece is simpler: agent boundaries can become latency boundaries. To protect that latency, responses are kept deliberately concise - across a 66-turn sample, the model averaged 34 words per reply and asked exactly one question 98% of the time. That’s not a coincidence either; avoiding cross-agent handoffs on every turn removes an additional source of latency from the critical path. What I actually built Source: Visual elements generated with Google Gemini The question became concrete while building an Android application that conducts real interviews through live voice . A candidate provides a job description and resume, then moves through technical, system-design, and behavioral rounds before receiving an evidence-backed evaluation. The implementation uses Agora for the real-time voice layer and a FastAPI backend for orchestration. The interesting architectural choice wasn’t that there were three roles - it was where their responsibilities stopped and the application took over. The backend uses a state-driven orchestrator to control the stages and maintain shared cross-round context, and zero AI calls are spent simply deciding whose turn it is. In production, a 70-turn interview requires exactly 70 LLM calls in the best-case scenario and zero additional routing calls; the orchestrator’s state-transition overhead averages 0.5ms, peaking at 1.3ms, while end-to-end voice latency - from the candidate finishing an utterance to hearing the interviewer’s response, is measured at 1.5–1.8 seconds. A role can be a boundary in behavior without being a boundary in computation. What this design costs None of this is free, and the friction is worth naming rather than only the upside. One model juggling three personas can bleed between them, a phrasing habit or a piece of context from the technical round leaking into the tone of the behavioral round if the prompt boundary isn’t reinforced turn by turn. Because there’s no hard module boundary, debugging “the system-design interviewer asked something odd” means inspecting the same context-construction code path that serves every other role, rather than isolating one agent’s logs. Evaluation gets harder to keep clean, too — since a persona is just instructions, a regression in one role’s behavior can be caused by a prompt change made for a completely different role, if they share a template. None of that is a reason to default to separate agents. It’s a reason to invest in strict per-turn context construction, per-persona regression tests, clear state transitions, isolated prompt configuration, and role-specific observability. That’s still cheaper than running three agents. So when should you create another agent? There are real cases where the boundary is genuine. If the technical interviewer needs to actually execute a candidate’s code, that component doesn’t just need a different personality - it needs different capabilities, different information boundaries, and different execution responsibilities. That’s a much stronger justification for an agent boundary. Before creating one, five questions are worth asking: Does it need a different model? Different tools? Genuinely different information or memory? A genuinely different objective? Does it need to execute independently? If the only honest answer is “it should behave differently,” a persona is probably enough. If several of the five come back yes, an agent boundary starts making real architectural sense. The architecture can evolve None of this has to be decided once and for all. A sensible system can start with one model, personas, a deterministic orchestrator, and shared memory - then grow into specialized tools, persistent memory, and asynchronous evaluation layered on top of the same core. Only later, once a specific role needs to execute code independently or take an irreversible external action, does that piece earn its own agent boundary. Scaling the number of users doesn’t automatically mean adding agents; if the application gets ten times more traffic, the first problems are almost always infrastructure problems - concurrency, queues, state storage, rate limits, model capacity, and none of those get solved by turning one agent into five. Scale is not the trigger for an agent boundary. Capability is. For this pipeline, that boundary hasn’t needed to move yet. The three interviewers still run on one reasoning system with three personas, a deterministic orchestrator, and shared memory, because none of the five questions above have come back yes for any of them. The day the technical round needs to actually execute a candidate’s code in a sandboxed runtime, that persona earns its own tools, its own state, and its own agent boundary. Until then, spinning it into a separate agent wouldn’t add a new capability - it would just add another network hop between the candidate and the next spoken word. The Agent Boundary Problem: Designing Multi-Role AI Systems with Memory and Orchestration was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

One model juggling three personas can bleed between them, a phrasing habit or a piece of context from the technical round leaking into the tone of the behavioral round if the prompt boundary isn’t reinforced turn by turn. Because there’s no hard module boundary, debugging “the system-design interviewer asked something odd” means inspecting the same context-construction code path that serves every other role, rather than isolating one agent’s logs. Evaluation gets harder to keep clean, too — since a persona is just instructions, a regression in one role’s behavior can be caused by a prompt change made for a completely different role, if they share a template.

None of that is a reason to default to separate agents. It’s a reason to invest in strict per-turn context construction, per-persona regression tests, clear state transitions, isolated prompt configuration, and role-specific observability. That’s still cheaper than running three agents.

So when should you create another agent?

There are real cases where the boundary is genuine. If the technical interviewer needs to actually execute a candidate’s code, that component doesn’t just need a different personality - it needs different capabilities, different information boundaries, and different execution responsibilities.

That’s a much stronger justification for an agent boundary. Before creating one, five questions are worth asking: Does it need a different model? Different tools? Genuinely different information or memory? A genuinely different objective? Does it need to execute independently? If the only honest answer is “it should behave differently,” a persona is probably enough. If several of the five come back yes, an agent boundary starts making real architectural sense.

The architecture can evolve

None of this has to be decided once and for all. A sensible system can start with one model, personas, a deterministic orchestrator, and shared memory - then grow into specialized tools, persistent memory, and asynchronous evaluation layered on top of the same core.

Only later, once a specific role needs to execute code independently or take an irreversible external action, does that piece earn its own agent boundary. Scaling the number of users doesn’t automatically mean adding agents; if the application gets ten times more traffic, the first problems are almost always infrastructure problems - concurrency, queues, state storage, rate limits, model capacity, and none of those get solved by turning one agent into five. Scale is not the trigger for an agent boundary. Capability is.

For this pipeline, that boundary hasn’t needed to move yet. The three interviewers still run on one reasoning system with three personas, a deterministic orchestrator, and shared memory, because none of the five questions above have come back yes for any of them. The day the technical round needs to actually execute a candidate’s code in a sandboxed runtime, that persona earns its own tools, its own state, and its own agent boundary. Until then, spinning it into a separate agent wouldn’t add a new capability - it would just add another network hop between the candidate and the next spoken word.

items.title: China Weighs Allowing Purchases of New Nvidia Chips by ByteDance, Alibaba
items.summary: China’s government has signaled it could allow some domestic companies to buy a new Nvidia chip built for high-end professional computers, according to two people familiar with the matter, as the country’s AI firms strain for enough computing power to run their chatbots and agents. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, which oversees China’s tech sector, recently asked companies including Alibaba Group and ByteDance to report on their plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips, released this month—specifically how many they want to buy and what they’ll use them for, the people said. The ministry has told some Chinese companies the government intends to approve the purchases, they said. Even if that happens, though, it’s unclear when the approvals would come, how many chips officials would allow and what standards they would use to decide.

items.title: Performance engineering from kernel analysis to AI: Adrian Cockcroft’s take
items.summary: Over its five-year history, P99 CONF has hosted quite a few speakers who’ve offered pointed takedowns of the namesake metric. At last year’s conference, Adrian Cockcroft didn’t explicitly state that P99s are BS … but he did allude to it. If you don’t know Cockcroft , he’s spent decades architecting, scaling, and optimizing resilient, high-performance systems at giants like Sun Microsystems, Netflix, eBay, and Amazon. We could probably dedicate an entire day of P99 CONF to discussing the lessons learned from just some of his projects (Solaris kernel performance, multi-processor optimization, Netflix’s on-prem to cloud migration, Chaos Monkey…) Fortunately, RedMonk analyst Rachel Stephens proved the perfect host for a conference that’s all about making things fast. She sat down with Adrian and led us on a whirlwind tour of how AI has impacted performance engineering. Here are some highlights from the chat (full video below). Note: P99 CONF 2026 – a free + virtual conference on all things performance – is going live October 21-22. Grab a complimentary pass and join us! From kernel analysis to vibe coding perf tools As a performance specialist at Sun in its heyday, getting to the root of performance problems involved lots of digging and divination. Cockcroft recalls, “Back in the old days with Sun, people would look at the output of system metrics in vmstat or whatever, and they’d be guessing what the numbers meant. There was a very vague understanding of what these things meant. The manual page wasn’t very clear.” Cockcroft ended up going to the source, literally. “I went and read all the kernel source code and figured out exactly where these numbers came from, exactly what they meant, which ones were approximating what, and wrote all that down.” That led to two performance books: Sun Performance and Tuning and Resource Management . “My speedup is infinite, because this code would never exist without these tools. I wouldn’t have the time to build them.” Four decades later, there’s now a wealth of helpful tools for end-to-end tracing, but Cockcroft’s curiosity still lies in what the tools are not showing. He continued, “Everything sort of looks okay in the tools – but the system isn’t behaving well. I usually come in and try to find a new way of looking at the data. A new type of analysis, or go a little bit deeper or finer grain, or stop looking at averages and start looking at distributions, and find all kinds of interesting things that nobody knew were happening.” Currently, he’s vibe coding tools to better analyze the anomalies he finds. Saved from having to brush up on Python or hunt down graphics library fragments on Stack Overflow, Cockcroft can now stand up custom tooling in minutes. “My speedup is infinite, because this code would never exist without these tools. I wouldn’t have the time to build them.” Peaks not percentiles One specific vibe coding project: Cockcroft built (and open-sourced) tooling to get a better understanding of response time distributions. Response time distributions have been on Cockcroft’s mind for over a decade. While most people obsess over percentiles – yes, P99 CONF included – Cockcroft is most intrigued by the distribution of response time peaks in a histogram. He believes percentiles don’t work when trying to understand the latency and performance of modern web services. A single number like P99 can’t tell you whether the underlying distribution has one peak or several. And when there’s more than one peak (as is often the case in the real world), the mean, the standard deviation, and even the P99 itself lose most of their meaning. “Percentiles don’t work when trying to understand the latency and performance of modern web services.” (source: A Tale of Two Histograms ) For example, assume you have a histogram with two response time peaks: a fast one from a cache hit and a slow one for misses that require actual work. As the cache hit rate shifts, each peak’s position remains the same (i.e., the latency values of the fast-response mode and the slow-response mode don’t change), but the peak heights rise and fall. “Your averages and your P99 are changing all over the place, but all that’s really happening is your cache hit rate is changing,” Cockcroft said. So how do you go beyond measuring P99s and averages? Cockcroft did what he’s done for decades: dive in and build a custom tool. But these days, it’s much simpler thanks to LLMs. “Your averages and your P99 are changing all over the place, but all that’s really happening is your cache hit rate is changing.” He had already worked out the statistical approach for analyzing the distribution. Once ChatGPT came out, he quickly used it to build a tool that automated it. Instead of collapsing everything into an average, it identifies an arbitrary number of peaks in a distribution and tracks how they fluctuate over time. It’s implemented in R – a language Cockcroft hadn’t used in a while, but ChatGPT knew quite well – and it’s open source . If you’re curious, learn more in his Percentiles Don’t Work article and “A Tale of Two Histograms” talk and deck (“ It was the best of response times, it was the worst of response times…”) Where do we go from here? To close, Stephens asked Cockcroft what advice he’d share with teams working on high-performance systems today. His top tip was to start with the macro view to find what’s interesting, then keep digging deeper until you’re inspecting individual slow requests end-to-end. “Remember the microscope that you got when you were a kid,” Cockcroft said. “First, you have to focus it using the lowest resolution, at 10x, and then you can click it to 100x and adjust that, looking at just one speck now. Once you get that in focus, you click it to 1,000x.” Cockcroft has spent his career building tools that bring obscure performance issues into focus. We look forward to seeing what others have cooked up with agentic tooling to help identify and solve performance problems this year at P99 CONF. Learn about the latest performance optimization techniques, tooling, and case studies at P99 CONF – free and virtual, October 21-22. Grab a complimentary pass and join us!

items.title: Before you pick a hosted agent runtime, check what happens at idle
items.summary: Disclosure: I work on Gobare, one of the three runtimes below. To keep that from mattering, I quote the other two instead of describing them, and there is a section on where each of us loses, Gobare included. All quotes are from public docs, checked 27 September 2026. Misha. I read the sandbox docs of three hosted agent runtimes side by side, ours included. In a 30-second demo they look the same. The agent writes code, runs it, shows a result. The difference is one question the demo never asks: After the agent stops typing, does its machine still exist? Perplexity, OpenAI and Gobare give three different answers. None of them is wrong. They are building different things. But if you pick one without checking, you find out an hour into a job, at the step where the work was supposed to land. This post is the check I wish I had done first. First, be clear which OpenAI product you mean OpenAI ships two things with similar names. They are not layers of each other. The Agents SDK is open source and runs in your process. You own the loop. Other models work through LiteLLM (Python) or the AI SDK adapter (TypeScript). The Agents API is hosted. OpenAI runs the loop, and it is built around OpenAI models. So "can I use Claude with OpenAI's agents?" has two answers. In the SDK, yes. In the hosted Agents API, the one that gives you a sandbox, non-OpenAI models are on a second-class path. Everything below is about hosted runtimes: the ones that give you a machine. Three answers, in their own words Perplexity , on their sandbox tool : "Multiple executions in a single response share the same container: files written and packages installed by an earlier step are still there for a later one." Between responses, nothing is promised. That is the right design for an answer engine that computes. If you want an answer, paying to keep a machine alive afterwards is waste. OpenAI , on hosted sandboxes : "If activity and keep-alives stop for an hour, the sandbox can be deleted." Files you write to /workspace/outputs become immutable artifacts that "remain downloadable after the sandbox expires." The rest of the workspace does not survive. Clean contract: the sandbox is a place to do work, not to keep it. Gobare , on limits : "A workspace is also paused after five minutes with nothing happening, and woken by the next thing you send." Before the machine is reclaimed, the workspace files are snapshotted. It is best-effort. Git history, installed dependencies and running processes are not in the snapshot, and a workspace over 300MB is skipped. Side by side: Perplexity OpenAI hosted Gobare Machine lives for One response Until an hour with no activity or keep-alives Paused after five idle minutes, woken by your next message What survives Nothing promised between responses Files in /workspace/outputs , as artifacts Workspace files, best-effort snapshot What doesn't The container The rest of the workspace Git history, installed deps, running processes; workspaces over 300MB Three workloads where the answer decides things These are not failures of a bad runtime. They are where a correct runtime, picked for the wrong shape of work, gives you a system you cannot finish. A job longer than the idle window. Say a 40-minute refactor across several turns, with gaps while your dispatcher does something else. On a per-request container each response starts clean, so this can't be expressed. On a session sandbox it works, if you know exactly what "idle" means to your provider. A task that stops to ask a human. Approval mid-run means the machine waits, maybe for hours. Whether that wait is free, billed or impossible depends on how the runtime treats an idle machine. An agent that serves something. If the agent starts a preview server, the machine has to exist when the visitor arrives. That can be long after the agent stopped writing code. If the sandbox goes when execution ends, the preview URL goes with it. The container has a public price Perplexity publishes a price for the container itself, on their pricing page : "$0.03 per session (≤20-min billing window)" That is roughly $0.09 an hour for a managed container. It is the clearest public anchor I found for what hosted agent compute costs. It also explains the product. Perplexity's money is in the search index. For them, the runtime does not need to be profitable, and that sets the floor for everyone else. Where each one loses Perplexity: no session state across responses. If work has to survive a response boundary, you build that yourself on previous_response_id . OpenAI hosted: an hour of quiet and the working tree is gone. Only what you published to /workspace/outputs stays. Non-OpenAI models are second-class on the hosted path. OpenAI self-hosted: you own the lifecycle, so you also own its outages. With Daytona as the provider you must set auto_stop_interval=0 , or the sandbox stops mid-agent. Gobare: Single sandbox provider (E2B). No bring-your-own-compute. That is real lock-in, and the fairest criticism of us here. A workspace is reclaimed two hours of active time after it starts. Paused time doesn't count, but a turn still running at that point fails. No model fallback chain. Perplexity tries up to five models; we have nothing equivalent. Saved agents are not versioned. No search index. Questions to ask any runtime's docs Take this list to whichever runtime you are evaluating. Every item comes from a place where these three differ. Lifetime Within one response or turn, do executions share a container? Is anything promised between responses? How long can the machine sit idle before it is paused or deleted? What counts as activity? On self-hosted compute, does the provider's idle tracking see the agent's connection, or do I have to disable auto-stop? Is there a hard cap on session lifetime, and what happens to a turn that is running when it hits? State What survives the machine: nothing, an outputs folder, or the whole workspace? What is excluded? Git history, installed dependencies, running processes, anything over a size limit? Workload fit Can the machine wait hours for a human? Is that wait free, billed or impossible? Can something the agent serves stay reachable after it stops generating? Control Who runs the agent loop, me or the vendor? Which models are first-class on the hosted path? Can I bring my own compute? Is there a model fallback when a provider goes down? Are saved agent configurations versioned? Is there a published price for the container itself? The one question that sorts the rest Not "which runtime is best." Ask: After my agent stops typing, do I still need the machine? If no, a per-request container is the honest choice, and you shouldn't pay for more. Perplexity's model is the clean version of that. If yes, you are choosing between owning the compute yourself and having someone manage its state for you. Both are defensible. Not knowing which one you picked is not. Full version with every source link: gobare.dev/blog/agent-runtimes-disagree-on-what-a-session-is If you have run agents in production: which of these questions did you only learn to ask after something broke?

Perplexity, OpenAI and Gobare give three different answers. None of them is wrong. They are building different things. But if you pick one without checking, you find out an hour into a job, at the step where the work was supposed to land.

This post is the check I wish I had done first.

First, be clear which OpenAI product you mean

OpenAI ships two things with similar names. They are not layers of each other.

  • The Agents SDK is open source and runs in your process. You own the loop. Other models work through LiteLLM (Python) or the AI SDK adapter (TypeScript).
  • The Agents API is hosted. OpenAI runs the loop, and it is built around OpenAI models.

So "can I use Claude with OpenAI's agents?" has two answers. In the SDK, yes. In the hosted Agents API, the one that gives you a sandbox, non-OpenAI models are on a second-class path.

Everything below is about hosted runtimes: the ones that give you a machine.

Three answers, in their own words

Perplexity, on their sandbox tool:

"Multiple executions in a single response share the same container: files written and packages installed by an earlier step are still there for a later one."

Between responses, nothing is promised. That is the right design for an answer engine that computes. If you want an answer, paying to keep a machine alive afterwards is waste.

OpenAI, on hosted sandboxes:

"If activity and keep-alives stop for an hour, the sandbox can be deleted."

Files you write to /workspace/outputs become immutable artifacts that "remain downloadable after the sandbox expires." The rest of the workspace does not survive. Clean contract: the sandbox is a place to do work, not to keep it.

Gobare, on limits:

"A workspace is also paused after five minutes with nothing happening, and woken by the next thing you send."

Before the machine is reclaimed, the workspace files are snapshotted. It is best-effort. Git history, installed dependencies and running processes are not in the snapshot, and a workspace over 300MB is skipped.

Side by side:

Perplexity OpenAI hosted Gobare Machine lives for One response Until an hour with no activity or keep-alives Paused after five idle minutes, woken by your next message What survives Nothing promised between responses Files in /workspace/outputs, as artifacts Workspace files, best-effort snapshot What doesn't The container The rest of the workspace Git history, installed deps, running processes; workspaces over 300MB
Three workloads where the answer decides things

These are not failures of a bad runtime. They are where a correct runtime, picked for the wrong shape of work, gives you a system you cannot finish.

  1. A job longer than the idle window. Say a 40-minute refactor across several turns, with gaps while your dispatcher does something else. On a per-request container each response starts clean, so this can't be expressed. On a session sandbox it works, if you know exactly what "idle" means to your provider.
  2. A task that stops to ask a human. Approval mid-run means the machine waits, maybe for hours. Whether that wait is free, billed or impossible depends on how the runtime treats an idle machine.
  3. An agent that serves something. If the agent starts a preview server, the machine has to exist when the visitor arrives. That can be long after the agent stopped writing code. If the sandbox goes when execution ends, the preview URL goes with it.
The container has a public price

Perplexity publishes a price for the container itself, on their pricing page:

"$0.03 per session (≤20-min billing window)"

That is roughly $0.09 an hour for a managed container. It is the clearest public anchor I found for what hosted agent compute costs.

It also explains the product. Perplexity's money is in the search index. For them, the runtime does not need to be profitable, and that sets the floor for everyone else.

Where each one loses
  • Perplexity: no session state across responses. If work has to survive a response boundary, you build that yourself on previous_response_id.
  • OpenAI hosted: an hour of quiet and the working tree is gone. Only what you published to /workspace/outputs stays. Non-OpenAI models are second-class on the hosted path.
  • OpenAI self-hosted: you own the lifecycle, so you also own its outages. With Daytona as the provider you must set auto_stop_interval=0, or the sandbox stops mid-agent.
  • Gobare:
    • Single sandbox provider (E2B). No bring-your-own-compute. That is real lock-in, and the fairest criticism of us here.
    • A workspace is reclaimed two hours of active time after it starts. Paused time doesn't count, but a turn still running at that point fails.
    • No model fallback chain. Perplexity tries up to five models; we have nothing equivalent.
    • Saved agents are not versioned.
    • No search index.
Questions to ask any runtime's docs

Take this list to whichever runtime you are evaluating. Every item comes from a place where these three differ.

Lifetime

  • Within one response or turn, do executions share a container?
  • Is anything promised between responses?
  • How long can the machine sit idle before it is paused or deleted?
  • What counts as activity? On self-hosted compute, does the provider's idle tracking see the agent's connection, or do I have to disable auto-stop?
  • Is there a hard cap on session lifetime, and what happens to a turn that is running when it hits?

State

  • What survives the machine: nothing, an outputs folder, or the whole workspace?
  • What is excluded? Git history, installed dependencies, running processes, anything over a size limit?

Workload fit

  • Can the machine wait hours for a human? Is that wait free, billed or impossible?
  • Can something the agent serves stay reachable after it stops generating?

Control

  • Who runs the agent loop, me or the vendor?
  • Which models are first-class on the hosted path?
  • Can I bring my own compute?
  • Is there a model fallback when a provider goes down?
  • Are saved agent configurations versioned?
  • Is there a published price for the container itself?
The one question that sorts the rest

Not "which runtime is best." Ask:

After my agent stops typing, do I still need the machine?

If no, a per-request container is the honest choice, and you shouldn't pay for more. Perplexity's model is the clean version of that.

If yes, you are choosing between owning the compute yourself and having someone manage its state for you. Both are defensible. Not knowing which one you picked is not.

Full version with every source link: gobare.dev/blog/agent-runtimes-disagree-on-what-a-session-is

If you have run agents in production: which of these questions did you only learn to ask after something broke?

items.summary_html:
Why 95% of Enterprise AI Agents Never Reach Production (And the 3 Orchestration Boundaries That Kill Them)

Enterprise AI agents promise transformative automation, yet 95% never make it to production. The culprit isn't technology—it's orchestration. Three critical boundaries consistently derail deployments: context management, state persistence, and integration complexity.

The Production Gap

Organizations invest heavily in AI agent frameworks, build impressive prototypes, and then hit a wall. The gap between proof-of-concept and production isn't a technology problem—it's an architectural one.

Why Prototypes Fail at Scale
  1. Context Explosion: Agents work fine with 10 documents. They break with 10,000.
  2. State Drift: Without proper persistence, agents lose context mid-conversation or across sessions.
  3. Integration Chaos: Connecting to enterprise systems requires orchestration that most frameworks don't provide.
The 3 Orchestration Boundaries Boundary 1: Context Management

The Problem: Enterprise data is massive and unstructured. Agents need to:

  • Retrieve relevant context from millions of documents
  • Maintain conversation history without token explosion
  • Handle context switching between different domains

Why It Kills Agents: Most frameworks treat context as a simple prompt injection. Real enterprise systems need:

  • Semantic search with relevance scoring
  • Hierarchical context pruning
  • Dynamic context windows based on task complexity

The Solution: Implement a context orchestration layer that:

  • Uses vector databases for semantic retrieval
  • Implements sliding window context management
  • Prioritizes information by relevance and recency
Boundary 2: State Persistence

The Problem: Agents are stateless by default. Enterprise workflows require:

  • Multi-turn conversations across days or weeks
  • Audit trails for compliance
  • Rollback capabilities for failed operations

Why It Kills Agents: Without proper state management:

  • Agents repeat work or forget decisions
  • Compliance teams can't audit agent actions
  • Failed operations cascade into data inconsistency

The Solution: Build a state orchestration layer with:

  • Persistent memory stores (databases, not just RAM)
  • Event sourcing for audit trails
  • Transaction-like semantics for agent operations
Boundary 3: Integration Complexity

The Problem: Enterprise AI agents must integrate with:

  • Legacy systems (mainframes, databases)
  • Modern APIs (SaaS, microservices)
  • Real-time data streams

Why It Kills Agents: Integration frameworks are either:

  • Too rigid (only support specific systems)
  • Too loose (require custom code for each integration)
  • Too slow (can't handle real-time requirements)

The Solution: Implement an integration orchestration layer:

  • Standardized adapter patterns for common systems
  • Async/await patterns for real-time data
  • Circuit breakers and retry logic for resilience
The Orchestration Framework

Successful enterprise AI agents share a common architecture:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Agent Core (LLM + Logic)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    Orchestration Layer (3 Boundaries)   │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┐ │
│  │ Context  │  State   │ Integration  │ │
│  │ Manager  │ Manager  │ Manager      │ │
│  └──────────┴──────────┴──────────────┘ │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    Enterprise Systems & Data Sources    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
Key Takeaways

  1. Orchestration is non-negotiable: The gap between prototype and production is orchestration, not model capability.

  2. Three boundaries matter most: Context management, state persistence, and integration complexity are where 95% of projects fail.

  3. Architecture beats algorithms: A well-orchestrated agent with GPT-3.5 outperforms a poorly-orchestrated agent with GPT-4.

  4. Start with one boundary: Don't try to solve all three at once. Pick the most critical boundary for your use case and build a robust solution there first.

What's Next?

The future of enterprise AI isn't about better models—it's about better orchestration. Organizations that master these three boundaries will own the AI-driven enterprise.

The question isn't whether your organization will deploy AI agents. It's whether you'll solve the orchestration problem before your competitors do.

items.summary_html:
Why 95% of Enterprise AI Agents Never Reach Production

95% of enterprise AI agents die before prod.

Not because the models are bad.

Because orchestration boundaries silently corrupt context, desync state, and deadlock callbacks between agents.

One bad weekend can cost $47K before anyone notices.

The Real Problem

Enterprise AI agents fail not due to model limitations, but due to orchestration failures. When multiple agents operate across distributed systems, the boundaries between them become critical failure points:

  • Context Corruption: State information gets lost or corrupted as it passes between agent boundaries
  • State Desynchronization: Agents operate on stale or conflicting versions of truth
  • Callback Deadlocks: Asynchronous operations block indefinitely, cascading failures across the system
The Cost of Failure

A single orchestration failure in production can cost organizations $47K+ before detection and remediation. The financial impact compounds when:

  • Multiple agents are interdependent
  • State corruption goes undetected for hours or days
  • Rollback requires manual intervention across distributed systems
What Breaks First?

In production environments, orchestration failures typically manifest as:

  1. Silent context loss between agent handoffs
  2. State machines entering invalid states
  3. Callback timeouts and cascading failures
  4. Data inconsistency across agent boundaries
The Path Forward

Successful enterprise AI deployments require:

  • Explicit orchestration boundaries with validation
  • State synchronization protocols between agents
  • Comprehensive monitoring of inter-agent communication
  • Graceful degradation and circuit breaker patterns

items.title: Why Humanoid Robots Might Be the Future of Elder Care
items.summary: The US spends roughly $400 billion a year on long-term care, and for every 100 people over 65, only four formal caregivers exist. Humanoid robots like Abi, built by Andromeda to provide emotional companionship for dementia patients, are an early attempt to ease that pressure. Andromeda COO Jennifer Haroon, Brookings researcher Gopi Goda, 1X Chief Designer Dar Sleeper, and Nvidia's Kimberly Powell discuss whether robots can truly help solve the elder care crisis, or whether the technology still has too far to go. (Source: Bloomberg)
