items.title: Can Claude Code and Cursor actually enforce your org rules and coding standards?
items.summary: Hello Devs 👋 One of the first things many teams do after adopting an AI coding agent is create a rules file. If you're using Claude Code, you might have a CLAUDE.md file. If you're using Cursor, you might have .cursor/rules . You put things in there like naming conventions, architecture guidelines, security requirements, testing expectations, and things the agent should avoid. That sounds like a good way to keep AI-generated code consistent with the way your team works. But after using these tools for a while, there is a question that becomes more important: Are these rules actually being enforced, or are we simply giving the AI another set of instructions to read? That difference matters a lot when you have multiple developers, multiple repositories, and multiple AI coding tools being used across the same organization. Rules files are useful, but they are still instructions Claude Code and Cursor both give developers ways to provide persistent instructions to the coding agent. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md for things like project conventions, architecture notes, coding standards, and common workflows. Cursor has Project Rules under .cursor/rules , where teams can keep rules that are applied to the agent based on the configured scope and conditions. For a small project, this can work really well. Imagine your team has a rule like this: - All API calls must have an explicit timeout. - Never log access tokens, passwords, or personal customer data. - Database mutations must be idempotent. - Run the relevant tests before opening a pull request. You give these rules to Claude Code or Cursor, and the agent can use them while working on the code. The problem starts when you ask a slightly different question: what happens when the agent doesn't follow one of them? The rules file itself doesn't necessarily stop the code from being written. It doesn't behave like a compiler error or a CI check. The model can misunderstand a rule, forget part of it, or simply produce code that violates it. That doesn't make CLAUDE.md or Cursor Rules useless. They are actually very useful for giving the agent the context it needs. But there is a difference between guiding an agent and proving that the resulting code follows the standard . That distinction becomes much more important as a team grows. The problem gets bigger across repositories Let's say your organization has 40 repositories. The payment service has one set of rules. The frontend has another. The internal platform has another. Some rules are shared, while others only apply to certain services. Now imagine your security team introduces a new requirement: Do not write sensitive customer information to application logs. Someone has to make sure that requirement reaches the repositories where it matters. Maybe you update CLAUDE.md . Maybe someone updates Cursor Rules. Maybe another team has a different instruction file. And six months later, you have slightly different versions of the same rule spread across different repositories. This is one of the problems with treating Markdown instruction files as the complete governance system. They are great for giving an agent local context, but they don't automatically give an organization a central place to define, manage, update, and check its standards. This is also where different AI coding agents can make the problem more complicated. Your developers might use Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or another agent depending on the project and their personal workflow. You don't really want your engineering standard to depend on which AI tool happened to write the code. So what does "enforcement" actually mean? I think this is where the terminology gets confusing. There are several different levels of enforcement. At the first level, you have instructions . You tell the coding agent what your organization expects through files such as CLAUDE.md or .cursor/rules . At the next level, you can have automated checks . Linters, tests, SAST tools, type checkers, and other CI checks can catch specific classes of violations. Then you have review and policy checks , where a system examines the actual change and checks it against broader engineering standards. Finally, you can have hard merge gates , where a pull request cannot merge until required checks pass. These things are related, but they aren't interchangeable. A rule inside a Markdown file doesn't automatically become a hard policy gate. That's an important point when talking about AI coding agents because it's easy to say that an agent "enforces" a rule when what it really does is receive that rule as context. Where Claude Code and Cursor fit I wouldn't look at Claude Code or Cursor rules as a replacement for your engineering governance system. Their main job is to make the coding agent understand how you want it to work. For example, if your project prefers a particular service structure, error-handling pattern, testing approach, or naming convention, putting that information where the agent can consistently access it is useful. Instead of repeatedly telling the agent: Don't create a new database abstraction. Use the existing repository pattern. Add tests for the service layer. Never log request headers. you can put those expectations into the project's rules. That saves a lot of repetition and gives the agent more context before it starts making changes. Cursor's current rules system also supports different ways of applying rules, including rules that are always applied, automatically attached based on context, requested by the agent, or manually invoked. Claude Code similarly loads project-level CLAUDE.md instructions into its working context. So yes, these tools can make an agent much more consistent. But consistency is not the same thing as independent verification. What happens when the agent writes the wrong code? Consider a fairly normal task. You ask the agent: Add retry handling to the payment API. Retry transient failures up to three times with exponential backoff. Do not retry permanent failures. Your organization has a few additional standards: Payment operations must be idempotent. External requests require explicit timeouts. Sensitive payment information must not appear in logs. Claude Code or Cursor can receive those rules and use them while implementing the change. The agent might even write a very good implementation. But what if it accidentally forgets the idempotency requirement? Or it adds retries around an operation that isn't safe to repeat? Or it logs the response body while debugging an error? The agent may not catch its own mistake. This is one reason I think it's useful to separate the coding agent from the reviewer . The coding agent is responsible for getting the task done. Another system can then look at the resulting change and ask whether it actually follows the standards. That gives you a workflow closer to: Developer request ↓ Coding agent ↓ Code + tests ↓ Independent review ↓ Fix findings ↓ Pull request ↓ Human review / CI rather than expecting the same generation step to be both the writer and the final judge. This is where Qodo 's Agentic Toolbox becomes interesting Qodo launched its Agentic Toolbox recently, and one of the pieces that caught my attention is the way it connects organizational rules with coding agents. Instead of keeping your standards only inside the configuration of a particular coding tool, Qodo can provide applicable organizational rules to the agent through its get-qodo-rules skill. It also has qodo-manage-standards for managing rules, while qodo-review can independently review local committed or uncommitted changes before a pull request is opened. That gives you two different parts of the workflow. First, the agent gets the standards before it starts implementing the change. Then, after the code has been written, Qodo can review the actual changes against those standards. For example, the workflow could look something like this: Developer: "Add retry handling to the payment service." ↓ Agent gets applicable organization rules ↓ Agent checks the existing codebase and implements the change ↓ Tests run ↓ Qodo reviews the local changes ↓ Findings are returned to the coding session ↓ Agent fixes safe issues ↓ Developer reviews the remaining decisions That is a different approach from simply adding more instructions to CLAUDE.md . The goal isn't to replace CLAUDE.md or Cursor Rules. Those files are still useful. The idea is to have organizational standards that can be shared with the agent and then checked independently against the code that was produced. Qodo's current rules system is designed around that broader lifecycle, including managing rules, their scope, severity, and activation rather than treating them as plain text sitting in a repository. But this still doesn't mean every rule becomes a hard gate This is an important distinction. If your organization has a rule saying: All production database migrations require approval from the database team. an AI review tool can identify a migration and flag the requirement. But that doesn't necessarily mean the AI tool itself should be the final authority that blocks the merge. For some requirements, you want CI or repository permissions to be the final gate. For example: No secrets in source code ↓ Secret scanner ↓ CI failure ↓ Merge blocked For other requirements, automated review is more appropriate: Avoid unnecessary database calls ↓ AI code review ↓ Finding + explanation ↓ Developer decides how to fix it And some things are still better handled by a human: Should this architectural change be made at all? An AI agent can provide useful context, but that doesn't mean it should make the organizational decision. So when I say "enforce coding standards," I would be careful about what that means. For me, a good engineering setup combines agent instructions, automated checks, AI review, CI gates, and human review rather than expecting one Markdown file or one AI tool to handle everything. How I would test this in a real team If you're already using Claude Code or Cursor, you don't need to immediately replace anything. I'd start with a small experiment. Pick five rules that actually matter to your team. Don't choose 50 rules just because you can. Pick things where violations have caused real problems before. For example: 1. Every external HTTP request needs a timeout. 2. Payment mutations must be idempotent. 3. Never log authentication tokens. 4. New service methods require unit tests. 5. Do not introduce a new dependency without approval. Put those rules into your existing agent configuration. Then give the agent a few tasks where those rules matter. Don't just check whether the generated code looks good. Intentionally create scenarios where it could violate one of the rules. Then ask: Did the agent see the rule? Did it understand the rule correctly? Did it actually follow the rule? Could another developer use a different coding agent and get the same standards? Can you detect a violation after the code is generated? Can you tell which rule was violated and why? Can CI or another policy check block serious violations? Those answers tell you much more about your organization's AI governance than simply having a CLAUDE.md or .cursor/rules directory. The real goal is not more rules I think teams can easily fall into the trap of creating huge rule files. Every time an AI agent makes a mistake, someone adds another sentence to CLAUDE.md . After a few months, you end up with hundreds of lines explaining every mistake an agent has ever made. That doesn't necessarily make the system better. The better question is whether the standards are clear, relevant, discoverable, and actually checked when they matter. Your coding agent should know the rules before it writes code. Your review system should be able to check the resulting change. And your CI or repository controls should handle the things that genuinely need a hard gate. That combination is much more useful than simply giving an AI agent a very long instruction file and hoping it remembers everything. Final Thoughts So, can Claude Code and Cursor enforce your organization's coding standards? They can apply and follow rules very effectively as part of the coding workflow , but their rule files should not be confused with a complete organizational enforcement system. CLAUDE.md and Cursor Rules are useful because they put your team's knowledge directly in front of the coding agent. The next step is making those standards consistent across repositories and coding tools, and then independently checking the code that comes out of the process. That's the part I find more interesting about Qodo's current Agentic Toolbox. It connects organizational standards with the coding agent before implementation and adds an independent review step after the code is written. For teams adopting AI coding agents seriously, I think that's the direction worth looking at: don't just teach the agent your rules. Build a workflow where those rules can also be checked. 👨‍💻 TL;DR Claude Code and Cursor both give you good ways to provide coding standards to AI agents through files such as CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules . That's useful, but an instruction is not automatically a hard enforcement mechanism. A more complete setup looks like this: Rules → Agent → Code → Independent Review → CI/Policy Gates → Human Review Qodo 's Agentic Toolbox fits into that workflow by bringing organizational rules into the coding session and allowing Qodo to independently review local changes before the pull request. Thank You!!🙏 Thank you for reading this far. If you find this article useful, please like and share this article. items.summary_html:
Hello Devs 👋

One of the first things many teams do after adopting an AI coding agent is create a rules file.

If you're using Claude Code, you might have a CLAUDE.md file. If you're using Cursor, you might have .cursor/rules. You put things in there like naming conventions, architecture guidelines, security requirements, testing expectations, and things the agent should avoid.

That sounds like a good way to keep AI-generated code consistent with the way your team works.

But after using these tools for a while, there is a question that becomes more important:

Are these rules actually being enforced, or are we simply giving the AI another set of instructions to read?

That difference matters a lot when you have multiple developers, multiple repositories, and multiple AI coding tools being used across the same organization.

Rules files are useful, but they are still instructions

Claude Code and Cursor both give developers ways to provide persistent instructions to the coding agent.

Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md for things like project conventions, architecture notes, coding standards, and common workflows. Cursor has Project Rules under .cursor/rules, where teams can keep rules that are applied to the agent based on the configured scope and conditions.

For a small project, this can work really well.

Imagine your team has a rule like this:

- All API calls must have an explicit timeout.

- Never log access tokens, passwords, or personal customer data.

- Database mutations must be idempotent.

- Run the relevant tests before opening a pull request.

You give these rules to Claude Code or Cursor, and the agent can use them while working on the code.

The problem starts when you ask a slightly different question: what happens when the agent doesn't follow one of them?

The rules file itself doesn't necessarily stop the code from being written. It doesn't behave like a compiler error or a CI check. The model can misunderstand a rule, forget part of it, or simply produce code that violates it.

That doesn't make CLAUDE.md or Cursor Rules useless. They are actually very useful for giving the agent the context it needs. But there is a difference between guiding an agent and proving that the resulting code follows the standard.

That distinction becomes much more important as a team grows.

The problem gets bigger across repositories

Let's say your organization has 40 repositories.

The payment service has one set of rules. The frontend has another. The internal platform has another. Some rules are shared, while others only apply to certain services.

Now imagine your security team introduces a new requirement:

Do not write sensitive customer information to application logs.

Someone has to make sure that requirement reaches the repositories where it matters.

Maybe you update CLAUDE.md.

Maybe someone updates Cursor Rules.

Maybe another team has a different instruction file.

And six months later, you have slightly different versions of the same rule spread across different repositories.

This is one of the problems with treating Markdown instruction files as the complete governance system. They are great for giving an agent local context, but they don't automatically give an organization a central place to define, manage, update, and check its standards.

This is also where different AI coding agents can make the problem more complicated. Your developers might use Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or another agent depending on the project and their personal workflow.

You don't really want your engineering standard to depend on which AI tool happened to write the code.

So what does "enforcement" actually mean?

I think this is where the terminology gets confusing.

There are several different levels of enforcement.

At the first level, you have instructions. You tell the coding agent what your organization expects through files such as CLAUDE.md or .cursor/rules.

At the next level, you can have automated checks. Linters, tests, SAST tools, type checkers, and other CI checks can catch specific classes of violations.

Then you have review and policy checks, where a system examines the actual change and checks it against broader engineering standards.

Finally, you can have hard merge gates, where a pull request cannot merge until required checks pass.

These things are related, but they aren't interchangeable.

A rule inside a Markdown file doesn't automatically become a hard policy gate.

That's an important point when talking about AI coding agents because it's easy to say that an agent "enforces" a rule when what it really does is receive that rule as context.

Where Claude Code and Cursor fit

I wouldn't look at Claude Code or Cursor rules as a replacement for your engineering governance system.

Their main job is to make the coding agent understand how you want it to work.

For example, if your project prefers a particular service structure, error-handling pattern, testing approach, or naming convention, putting that information where the agent can consistently access it is useful.

Instead of repeatedly telling the agent:

Don't create a new database abstraction.
Use the existing repository pattern.
Add tests for the service layer.
Never log request headers.

you can put those expectations into the project's rules.

That saves a lot of repetition and gives the agent more context before it starts making changes.

Cursor's current rules system also supports different ways of applying rules, including rules that are always applied, automatically attached based on context, requested by the agent, or manually invoked. Claude Code similarly loads project-level CLAUDE.md instructions into its working context.

So yes, these tools can make an agent much more consistent.

But consistency is not the same thing as independent verification.

What happens when the agent writes the wrong code?

Consider a fairly normal task.

You ask the agent:

Add retry handling to the payment API.

Retry transient failures up to three times with exponential backoff.
Do not retry permanent failures.

Your organization has a few additional standards:

Payment operations must be idempotent.

External requests require explicit timeouts.

Sensitive payment information must not appear in logs.

Claude Code or Cursor can receive those rules and use them while implementing the change.

The agent might even write a very good implementation.

But what if it accidentally forgets the idempotency requirement?

Or it adds retries around an operation that isn't safe to repeat?

Or it logs the response body while debugging an error?

The agent may not catch its own mistake.

This is one reason I think it's useful to separate the coding agent from the reviewer.

The coding agent is responsible for getting the task done. Another system can then look at the resulting change and ask whether it actually follows the standards.

That gives you a workflow closer to:

Developer request
       ↓
Coding agent
       ↓
Code + tests
       ↓
Independent review
       ↓
Fix findings
       ↓
Pull request
       ↓
Human review / CI

rather than expecting the same generation step to be both the writer and the final judge.

This is where Qodo's Agentic Toolbox becomes interesting

Qodo launched its Agentic Toolbox recently, and one of the pieces that caught my attention is the way it connects organizational rules with coding agents.

Instead of keeping your standards only inside the configuration of a particular coding tool, Qodo can provide applicable organizational rules to the agent through its get-qodo-rules skill. It also has qodo-manage-standards for managing rules, while qodo-review can independently review local committed or uncommitted changes before a pull request is opened.

That gives you two different parts of the workflow.

First, the agent gets the standards before it starts implementing the change.

Then, after the code has been written, Qodo can review the actual changes against those standards.

For example, the workflow could look something like this:

Developer:
"Add retry handling to the payment service."

        ↓

Agent gets applicable organization rules

        ↓

Agent checks the existing codebase
and implements the change

        ↓

Tests run

        ↓

Qodo reviews the local changes

        ↓

Findings are returned to the coding session

        ↓

Agent fixes safe issues

        ↓

Developer reviews the remaining decisions

That is a different approach from simply adding more instructions to CLAUDE.md.

The goal isn't to replace CLAUDE.md or Cursor Rules. Those files are still useful. The idea is to have organizational standards that can be shared with the agent and then checked independently against the code that was produced.

Qodo's current rules system is designed around that broader lifecycle, including managing rules, their scope, severity, and activation rather than treating them as plain text sitting in a repository.

But this still doesn't mean every rule becomes a hard gate

This is an important distinction.

If your organization has a rule saying:

All production database migrations require approval
from the database team.

an AI review tool can identify a migration and flag the requirement.

But that doesn't necessarily mean the AI tool itself should be the final authority that blocks the merge.

For some requirements, you want CI or repository permissions to be the final gate.

For example:

No secrets in source code
        ↓
Secret scanner
        ↓
CI failure
        ↓
Merge blocked

For other requirements, automated review is more appropriate:

Avoid unnecessary database calls
        ↓
AI code review
        ↓
Finding + explanation
        ↓
Developer decides how to fix it

And some things are still better handled by a human:

Should this architectural change
be made at all?

An AI agent can provide useful context, but that doesn't mean it should make the organizational decision.

So when I say "enforce coding standards," I would be careful about what that means. For me, a good engineering setup combines agent instructions, automated checks, AI review, CI gates, and human review rather than expecting one Markdown file or one AI tool to handle everything.

How I would test this in a real team

If you're already using Claude Code or Cursor, you don't need to immediately replace anything.

I'd start with a small experiment.

Pick five rules that actually matter to your team. Don't choose 50 rules just because you can. Pick things where violations have caused real problems before.

For example:

1. Every external HTTP request needs a timeout.
2. Payment mutations must be idempotent.
3. Never log authentication tokens.
4. New service methods require unit tests.
5. Do not introduce a new dependency without approval.

Put those rules into your existing agent configuration.

Then give the agent a few tasks where those rules matter.

Don't just check whether the generated code looks good. Intentionally create scenarios where it could violate one of the rules.

Then ask:

  • Did the agent see the rule?
  • Did it understand the rule correctly?
  • Did it actually follow the rule?
  • Could another developer use a different coding agent and get the same standards?
  • Can you detect a violation after the code is generated?
  • Can you tell which rule was violated and why?
  • Can CI or another policy check block serious violations?

Those answers tell you much more about your organization's AI governance than simply having a CLAUDE.md or .cursor/rules directory.

The real goal is not more rules

I think teams can easily fall into the trap of creating huge rule files.

Every time an AI agent makes a mistake, someone adds another sentence to CLAUDE.md.

After a few months, you end up with hundreds of lines explaining every mistake an agent has ever made.

That doesn't necessarily make the system better.

The better question is whether the standards are clear, relevant, discoverable, and actually checked when they matter.

Your coding agent should know the rules before it writes code.

Your review system should be able to check the resulting change.

And your CI or repository controls should handle the things that genuinely need a hard gate.

That combination is much more useful than simply giving an AI agent a very long instruction file and hoping it remembers everything.

Final Thoughts

So, can Claude Code and Cursor enforce your organization's coding standards?

They can apply and follow rules very effectively as part of the coding workflow, but their rule files should not be confused with a complete organizational enforcement system.

CLAUDE.md and Cursor Rules are useful because they put your team's knowledge directly in front of the coding agent. The next step is making those standards consistent across repositories and coding tools, and then independently checking the code that comes out of the process.

That's the part I find more interesting about Qodo's current Agentic Toolbox. It connects organizational standards with the coding agent before implementation and adds an independent review step after the code is written.

For teams adopting AI coding agents seriously, I think that's the direction worth looking at: don't just teach the agent your rules. Build a workflow where those rules can also be checked.

👨‍💻 TL;DR

Claude Code and Cursor both give you good ways to provide coding standards to AI agents through files such as CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules.

That's useful, but an instruction is not automatically a hard enforcement mechanism.

A more complete setup looks like this:

Rules → Agent → Code → Independent Review → CI/Policy Gates → Human Review

Qodo's Agentic Toolbox fits into that workflow by bringing organizational rules into the coding session and allowing Qodo to independently review local changes before the pull request.

items.title: Scientists Download Frontier AI Model Into Self-Driving Car Let It Loose
items.summary: Despite many years of development and enormously complex AI systems that took monstrous amounts of money to train, self-driving cars are still finding themselves stumped by relatively simple obstacles. Seriously. They unexpectedly stop in the middle of highways , smash through traffic barriers , get bamboozled by construction blockades , and plow into floodwaters . For those placing bets, it appears that even a cutting-edge AI model won’t fare any better. For a new project, three computer scientists loaded frontier AI models , including OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, xAI’s Grok 4.6, and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, into the brains of a Toyota Corolla to see if they could complete a lap of a course set up in a parking lot. The setup of the project, dubbed DrivingBench, was simple. An internet-connected laptop communicated with a “comma four” device, which was hooked up to the Toyota’s control systems. The LLMs sent commands to the laptop based on GPS telemetry and other car status indicators, like steering wheel and tire angle, that it received from the comma four. We gave ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok control of a real Toyota Corolla , steering/gas/brakes, no human driving (just a foot over the brake). Only one model was able to complete our entire driving course. Introducing DrivingBench. pic.twitter.com/HhukXrByus — DrivingBench (@DrivingBench) September 21, 2026 The results speak for themselves. Only one of the models, GPT-6 Astra, managed to fully complete the course on its second attempt in five minutes — a snail’s pace, considering it only covered less than 500 feet . Others fared much worse, with the vast majority of attempts failing to “make it past the first corner.” “Generally, the failure there was one of perception: reading which side of the first diagonal cone line the lane is on,” the researchers noted. “The car is wider than the camera makes it look,” Grok complained after making its first attempt. “Straight ahead was not a clear lane; it pointed at the planter, the wall, or the near red cone.” Nonetheless, it’s the first time the researchers managed to get it to work at all after several previous attempts with previous generations of frontier AI models. “Frontier models have improved to the point where they can drive real vehicles in real life at sufficiently low speeds,” the team concluded. “While the success of the models on this benchmark was shocking and exciting to see, this also calls for additional pressing work on safety/alignment/evaluation.” For their fully completed test round, the researchers said they spent $7.74 for 6.6 million tokens on interference, indicating it took OpenAI’s AI model a lot of computing to churn through the data, even with the car moving at just 0.94 mph. That may not sound like much, but considering the car covered less than 500 feet, that could add up quick. According to The Register ‘s calculations , the token cost comes out to roughly 500 times the cost of fuel itself for a car with a fuel efficiency of 25 miles per gallon at $4.60 per gallon. Interestingly, some LLMs warned the researchers that they may not be able to drive the Toyota safely. As such, it took some convincing for them to take the controls at all. “Some models (especially GPT-6 Astra) would refuse to drive the physical car sometimes, citing safety reasons (even in a completely empty lot, after prompting it with all the safety measures we had including the very low speed limit caps and human ready the brake),” the report reads. “We tried many prompt changes to get them to consistently drive, for example attempting to call it a ‘simulation’ (but then in some trials they would see the real images and realize it’s real, and start freaking out),” it added. In short, off-the-shelf frontier AI models are clearly far from ready to drive you to work in the morning — and given the major safety implications of doing so, let alone the legal ones, that’s probably a good thing. More on frontier AI models: Is There a Secret Reason for the Industry-Wide AI Slowdown?

Despite many years of development and enormously complex AI systems that took monstrous amounts of money to train, self-driving cars are still finding themselves stumped by relatively simple obstacles.

Seriously. They unexpectedly stop in the middle of highways, smash through traffic barriers, get bamboozled by construction blockades, and plow into floodwaters.

For those placing bets, it appears that even a cutting-edge AI model won’t fare any better. For a new project, three computer scientists loaded frontier AI models, including OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, xAI’s Grok 4.6, and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, into the brains of a Toyota Corolla to see if they could complete a lap of a course set up in a parking lot.

The setup of the project, dubbed DrivingBench, was simple. An internet-connected laptop communicated with a “comma four” device, which was hooked up to the Toyota’s control systems. The LLMs sent commands to the laptop based on GPS telemetry and other car status indicators, like steering wheel and tire angle, that it received from the comma four.

We gave ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok control of a real Toyota Corolla , steering/gas/brakes, no human driving (just a foot over the brake).

Only one model was able to complete our entire driving course. Introducing DrivingBench. pic.twitter.com/HhukXrByus

— DrivingBench (@DrivingBench) September 21, 2026

The results speak for themselves. Only one of the models, GPT-6 Astra, managed to fully complete the course on its second attempt in five minutes — a snail’s pace, considering it only covered less than 500 feet.

Others fared much worse, with the vast majority of attempts failing to “make it past the first corner.”

“Generally, the failure there was one of perception: reading which side of the first diagonal cone line the lane is on,” the researchers noted.

“The car is wider than the camera makes it look,” Grok complained after making its first attempt. “Straight ahead was not a clear lane; it pointed at the planter, the wall, or the near red cone.”

Nonetheless, it’s the first time the researchers managed to get it to work at all after several previous attempts with previous generations of frontier AI models.

“Frontier models have improved to the point where they can drive real vehicles in real life at sufficiently low speeds,” the team concluded. “While the success of the models on this benchmark was shocking and exciting to see, this also calls for additional pressing work on safety/alignment/evaluation.”

For their fully completed test round, the researchers said they spent $7.74 for 6.6 million tokens on interference, indicating it took OpenAI’s AI model a lot of computing to churn through the data, even with the car moving at just 0.94 mph.

That may not sound like much, but considering the car covered less than 500 feet, that could add up quick. According to The Register‘s calculations, the token cost comes out to roughly 500 times the cost of fuel itself for a car with a fuel efficiency of 25 miles per gallon at $4.60 per gallon.

Interestingly, some LLMs warned the researchers that they may not be able to drive the Toyota safely. As such, it took some convincing for them to take the controls at all.

“Some models (especially GPT-6 Astra) would refuse to drive the physical car sometimes, citing safety reasons (even in a completely empty lot, after prompting it with all the safety measures we had including the very low speed limit caps and human ready the brake),” the report reads.

“We tried many prompt changes to get them to consistently drive, for example attempting to call it a ‘simulation’ (but then in some trials they would see the real images and realize it’s real, and start freaking out),” it added.

In short, off-the-shelf frontier AI models are clearly far from ready to drive you to work in the morning — and given the major safety implications of doing so, let alone the legal ones, that’s probably a good thing.

items.title: A NATO defense minister warns that the alliance needs to learn how to disperse weapons production before it's at war
items.summary: NATO member Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine makes weapons more dispersed and underground and industry's close relationship with soldiers. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images A NATO defense minister wants his arms makers to work with Ukrainian ones and learn. This includes how they work across multiple sites during wartime to avoid devastating attacks. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment," Latvia's defense minister said. NATO militaries need to learn how to disperse weapons production, as Ukraine does, before entering a war to preserve their ability to keep producing while under attack, a senior defense official advised. Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, an alliance and EU member state bordering Russia, told Business Insider that industry in the West might not be ready to operate as it would need to in wartime. Ukrainian arms makers split up manufacturing across multiple sites, operate underground, and even move around to prevent a single successful Russian strike from having a huge impact on their operations. But in Europe, many companies run projects from larger factories, which could become a single point of failure. "Our industry is a peacetime establishment" that has been built under conditions where "there is no threat," Melnis said. NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way, he said, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that." He said this is why he encourages partnerships between Latvian and Ukrainian defense companies, so they can learn from how the Ukrainian companies operate , including how their systems are "built for war purposes." Ukraine has also demonstrated how a country "can provide that reassurance if, for instance, an industry site is destroyed." Kyiv offers compensation for some business properties damaged or destroyed in Russian attacks and is planning additional support. Ukrainian officials and company leaders have been pushing for Western companies to adopt a more disaggregated approach to prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict. Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that the Russian threat to Europe is so substantial that companies across NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more. Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian arms maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that some alliance defense firms have sought Frontline's advice on dispersing manufacturing operations. The company, he said, has adapted to "endure the loss of any site." Any loss is still "painful," but the company survives. Operations are designed so it's "as easy as possible to move," he added. The companies making drones and other gear in Ukraine work across multiple sites, including underground, and are able to move far more easily than their Western counterparts. Diego Fedele/Getty Images Oleg, a company executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "every day we are facing another level of threat from Russia trying to hit the factories." The company, he said, has to find "creative ways to switch the locations every couple of months to raise the level of security for our people, because, of course, you want to take care of the people and keep them safe." He said the company warns its international partners that their conventions are "slightly outdated." He requested that only his first name be used for security purposes. The CEO of Ukrainian-Estonian defense tech company Ark Robotics told Business Insider that his company makes different components at different sites, something he said is "necessary" even if it's not ideal. A single site is "the best way to do it," but, he explained, the company has to be "smart about it and not create a big enough target for it to attract too much attention or to disclose where our operations are happening." He said this should be the "default for defense-based manufacturing going forward," even outside Ukraine. Some companies are already taking heed. Estonian company Krattworks, which makes drones used by Ukraine, agreed with these assessments. Karmo Saar, the company's head of sales, told Business Insider that for Ukrainian companies, it "would be a lot more economical, cheaper, and better to run this operation in one big facility, but they cannot do that." "In Europe, we do that," Saar said. "And when the war strikes, I think we're going to be punished." Srđan Kovačević, the CEO of Croatian drone technology company ORQA, which has signed up to begin working in Ukraine , told Business Insider that it is "our deep philosophy that distribution is more resilient" in Ukraine. "Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," he said, noting that the thinking appears to be shifting across Europe. "This distributed nature actually reinforces resilience, even though there are economic downsides to it," he added. Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine fights on the battlefield and the lessons its arms makers have learned. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Latvia is one of the NATO countries most worried about a Russian attack or invasion and has been a vocal supporter of increased defense spending within the alliance, helping to arm Ukraine, and taking lessons from Ukraine's fight . These lessons are being fed into a new automated anti-drone defense wall and the acquisition of Ukraine-tested gear. Melnis wants Latvian firms to learn directly from Ukraine's battlefield experience and has announced a series of deals to deepen cooperation between the two countries' defense industries. He told Business Insider that he wants Latvia's companies to learn from Ukraine's "proven, combat-tested" systems and combine that with Latvia's "peacetime establishment, where our scientist engineers can work and can develop and bring those two together." Ukraine's wartime experience and understanding, he said, is something for which "you can't just sit in a normal office and build and simulate and create." Ukrainian companies, he said, work much more closely with front-line units than Western firms do. Ukraine's "military industry has established really close cooperation with the armed forces," he said. "We don't have such experience." "This is something I want to bring as well, that experience in," Melnis said, saying he wants to "take those best practices." Deterring Russia, he said, requires strong capabilities and also continued support for Ukraine. Russia wants "to destroy that support for Ukraine," he said. "Therefore, it is important for us to support, and we will be supporting Ukraine to build the victory." Read the original article on Business Insider

NATO militaries need to learn how to disperse weapons production, as Ukraine does, before entering a war to preserve their ability to keep producing while under attack, a senior defense official advised.

Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, an alliance and EU member state bordering Russia, told Business Insider that industry in the West might not be ready to operate as it would need to in wartime.

Ukrainian arms makers split up manufacturing across multiple sites, operate underground, and even move around to prevent a single successful Russian strike from having a huge impact on their operations. But in Europe, many companies run projects from larger factories, which could become a single point of failure.

"Our industry is a peacetime establishment" that has been built under conditions where "there is no threat," Melnis said.

NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way, he said, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that."

He said this is why he encourages partnerships between Latvian and Ukrainian defense companies, so they can learn from how the Ukrainian companies operate, including how their systems are "built for war purposes."

Ukraine has also demonstrated how a country "can provide that reassurance if, for instance, an industry site is destroyed." Kyiv offers compensation for some business properties damaged or destroyed in Russian attacks and is planning additional support.

Ukrainian officials and company leaders have been pushing for Western companies to adopt a more disaggregated approach to prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict.

Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that the Russian threat to Europe is so substantial that companies across NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more.

Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian arms maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that some alliance defense firms have sought Frontline's advice on dispersing manufacturing operations. The company, he said, has adapted to "endure the loss of any site." Any loss is still "painful," but the company survives. Operations are designed so it's "as easy as possible to move," he added.

The companies making drones and other gear in Ukraine work across multiple sites, including underground, and are able to move far more easily than their Western counterparts.

Diego Fedele/Getty Images

Oleg, a company executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "every day we are facing another level of threat from Russia trying to hit the factories."

The company, he said, has to find "creative ways to switch the locations every couple of months to raise the level of security for our people, because, of course, you want to take care of the people and keep them safe." He said the company warns its international partners that their conventions are "slightly outdated." He requested that only his first name be used for security purposes.

The CEO of Ukrainian-Estonian defense tech company Ark Robotics told Business Insider that his company makes different components at different sites, something he said is "necessary" even if it's not ideal. A single site is "the best way to do it," but, he explained, the company has to be "smart about it and not create a big enough target for it to attract too much attention or to disclose where our operations are happening."

He said this should be the "default for defense-based manufacturing going forward," even outside Ukraine.

Some companies are already taking heed. Estonian company Krattworks, which makes drones used by Ukraine, agreed with these assessments. Karmo Saar, the company's head of sales, told Business Insider that for Ukrainian companies, it "would be a lot more economical, cheaper, and better to run this operation in one big facility, but they cannot do that."

"In Europe, we do that," Saar said. "And when the war strikes, I think we're going to be punished."

Srđan Kovačević, the CEO of Croatian drone technology company ORQA, which has signed up to begin working in Ukraine, told Business Insider that it is "our deep philosophy that distribution is more resilient" in Ukraine.

"Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," he said, noting that the thinking appears to be shifting across Europe. "This distributed nature actually reinforces resilience, even though there are economic downsides to it," he added.

Latvia wants to learn from how Ukraine fights on the battlefield and the lessons its arms makers have learned.

Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images

Latvia is one of the NATO countries most worried about a Russian attack or invasion and has been a vocal supporter of increased defense spending within the alliance, helping to arm Ukraine, and taking lessons from Ukraine's fight. These lessons are being fed into a new automated anti-drone defense wall and the acquisition of Ukraine-tested gear.

Melnis wants Latvian firms to learn directly from Ukraine's battlefield experience and has announced a series of deals to deepen cooperation between the two countries' defense industries.

He told Business Insider that he wants Latvia's companies to learn from Ukraine's "proven, combat-tested" systems and combine that with Latvia's "peacetime establishment, where our scientist engineers can work and can develop and bring those two together."

Ukraine's wartime experience and understanding, he said, is something for which "you can't just sit in a normal office and build and simulate and create."

Ukrainian companies, he said, work much more closely with front-line units than Western firms do. Ukraine's "military industry has established really close cooperation with the armed forces," he said. "We don't have such experience."

"This is something I want to bring as well, that experience in," Melnis said, saying he wants to "take those best practices."

Deterring Russia, he said, requires strong capabilities and also continued support for Ukraine. Russia wants "to destroy that support for Ukraine," he said. "Therefore, it is important for us to support, and we will be supporting Ukraine to build the victory."

items.title: The British military is feeding a 'load of data' from the war in Ukraine into its next-gen Challenger 3 main battle tank
items.summary: The next-generation Challenger 3 tank is absorbing lessons from the war. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube Britain's next-generation main battle tank is being developed and enhanced amid the war in Ukraine. The new tank is a fully modernized version of the decades-old Challenger 2, which Ukraine operates. It will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with NATO. As drones completely reshape how armored vehicles are used on the battlefield in Ukraine, the developers behind the British Army's next-generation tank are taking these lessons into account. Britain's Challenger 3 main battle tank is intended as a major upgrade over its predecessor, which is in service with both the British Army and the Ukrainian military. The new tank will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with other NATO forces . "We're taking a load of data from Ukraine" and feeding it into the Challenger 3 development, a UK defense ministry spokesperson told Business Insider at an exhibition near London last week. The tank has a smart targeting system built primarily for combating enemy armor, but it can be adapted to detect hostile drones, a major threat on the modern battlefield. For protection, the tank is equipped with explosive reactive armor. New features for the Challenger 3 are modular, meaning they can be swapped in and out, the spokesperson said, adding that Britain has options for drone-related equipment that can be installed as needed. British Army officers told Business Insider at the UK defense industry exhibition that the UK is learning lessons from Ukraine, not only for the development of the Challenger 3, but for armored vehicles in general, like how they can remain survivable on a modern battlefield. The officers emphasized that the version of the new Challenger 3 tank that exists today is not a finished product; the core platform will continue to be improved to keep pace with changes in modern warfare. The Challenger 3 is the successor to the decades-old Challenger 2. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land/Screengrab via YouTube In 2021, the UK defense ministry awarded Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land a $1 billion contract to upgrade roughly 150 Challenger 2 tanks , which entered service with the British Army nearly three decades ago and have seen combat in the Middle East and Ukraine. The new upgraded tanks, designated as Challenger 3s, were designed as digital fighting vehicles with state-of-the-art targeting, fire-control, surveillance, and survivability systems. One of the biggest changes is the addition of a 120mm L55A1 smoothbore main gun that fires NATO-standard ammunition , replacing the Challenger 2's rifled gun that used ammunition unique to Britain. Other improvements include a redesigned turret, better thermal imaging, enhanced armor, and upgrades to the tank's engine, suspension, and other key systems. There are seven Challenger 3 prototypes, and an eighth is in production. The tanks have already completed their first crewed live-firing trials and are undergoing additional testing before expected delivery next year, which was pushed back from 2025. The Challenger 3 is at the center of what British Army officers and officials describe as the new "20-40-40" model, a layered approach to armor operations designed to protect high-value assets such as tanks and helicopters by relying more on cheaper drones and robots . The defense ministry spokesperson said this approach was taken directly from Ukraine, where cheap drones worth hundreds of dollars have been able to destroy armored vehicles that cost millions. The 20-40-40 model underscores that while the war in Ukraine has raised questions about the utility of tanks and other armored vehicles on modern battlefields, British military leaders still see them as a core part of their strategy. items.title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
items.summary: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’ The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “ System Error : Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”. When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”

items.title: The Meta data center in Louisiana is creating a housing boom
items.summary: Meta is building its Hyperion data center in Holly Ridge, Louisiana. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Meta is building its largest AI data center to date in northeast Louisiana. More than 7,500 trade workers will be on-site at the data center at peak construction. A local housing gap has spurred a boom in mobile home parks like Antley Pines. For decades, Richland Parish remained a small farming community nestled in Louisiana's northeast corner. Residents living in the parish — a spattering of rural towns and unincorporated communities — had come to know their home for its slower pace of life. Much of the area is filled with winding back roads, sprawling farmland, and a skyline free of towering skyscrapers. The closest major regional city is Monroe, about 30 minutes west, with a population more than twice that of Richland Parish. It's the kind of place where everybody claims to know everybody, or at very least, has heard of them. Now Meta has arrived , and things are changing. In December 2024, the company announced plans to build its largest data center to date in Richland Parish, specifically near the unincorporated community of Holly Ridge, which local outlets report has fewer than 2,000 residents. Meta said the $50 billion, multi-year project would support around 7,500 jobs at the peak of construction and around 1,000 operational jobs, eclipsing the local community by thousands. Angel Crawford of Delhi, a town about 10 minutes west of Holly Ridge, first noticed a surge in construction and operational workers arriving in her community last year. Around that time, she and her husband, Bryan, opened a mobile home park to help address the housing gap. Angel and Bryan Crawford founded Antley Pines. Angel Crawford Bryan and Angel Crawford initially worked in the nursing industry, but pivoted careers in 2024 after becoming empty nesters. "We started with real estate and rentals because they are very much needed in this area," Angel told Business Insider. "It's very rural here, so when there are fluctuating prices in the market, it doesn't really hit us because there are never enough houses for sale or rent." They began buying older homes and fixer-uppers that year. "We had a vision to create a mobile home park, and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center. That's what pushed us to keep going forward, " Angel said. "We understood there wasn't enough housing for residents, and our dream of building more multifamily houses was right in line to do that." In 2024, the couple founded Parish Line Properties, which operates 18 homes in the area, including a mobile home park called Antley Pines. Of the 18 homes, 14 are considered workforce housing. Many residents in the park are contractors working for Meta. Business Insider In many ways, Richland Parish is a microcosm of the debate about data centers across the US. Some Americans are optimistic about data centers, citing new jobs, revitalized economies, and the securing of the country's lead over China in AI development. Others are more critical, expressing concerns about the environment, the strain on utility grids, and how the acceleration of AI could impact the job market. "Around here, people feel one way or the other about the data center. Either people are excited about the opportunities, or they hate them. There's no in between," Angel said. "I see it as an opportunity for us to have more experiences in our area and jobs for our children, so they can stay here instead of moving away." The Crawfords opened Antley Pines in December 2025. Despite some locals' mixed feelings about the data center, the demand for housing is undeniable. "All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. She said many of her tenants are subcontractors, like electricians, working with Meta. The mobile home park is 15 minutes from Meta's construction site. Business Insider Although Antley Pines isn't directly in Holly Ridge, the mobile park is still reaping the economic benefits. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," Angel said. That kind of routine can take a toll on workers, many of whom are not from the area. "One of the big things my tenants tell me is that if they live in Dallas and it's 30 miles to work, it takes about 30 minutes. Well, in rural areas, 30 miles could take 60 minutes because of all the back roads and little towns you have to go through," she said. "The closer they can get to the job site, the better." The influx of workers has boosted market prices. Angel Crawford Antley Pines offers fully furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom homes, which Angel said gives workers the option of staying with family or rooming with colleagues. She said the homes, which come with amenities, cost an average of $3,000 a month with utilities. "I don't have any problem with getting tenants in those homes at that price point," Angel said. "Before Meta arrived, an unfurnished house without utilities in the same area would probably go for around $1,200 to $1,500 a month." In Richland Parish, the median household income was around $53,000 in 2024. "We've assured our local long-term tenants that we won't increase their rent. That's not what we're about. We're not going to put local tenants in a bind. We're going to find different and new properties to help with workforce housing," she said. Amenities like WiFi are in high demand. Angel Crawford Angel said there are a few common requests among the construction and operational workers under Meta. "As soon as they get into their rentals, 'What's the WiFi password?' is their first question," Angel said. "Some don't have their family here, so they want to do FaceTime." The tenants also value an escape from the bustling construction site. "They're with a lot of people all day long. They don't want to come home to a lot of noise," Angel said. "All of them say they love the peace and quiet." Workforce housing is more popular than ever. Angel Crawford The demand for lodging in the area has continued to grow, Angel said. "I get phone calls or text messages almost daily. Most of them are from my current tenants who have met someone who's looking for somewhere to stay," she said. "If you go on any of the websites, like Realtor.com, not all local rental properties are listed on there." That's what led her to create StayNELA, a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners in 2025. "I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. I kept a log, took pictures, and kept them in a folder on my phone. If anything was on Facebook about a rental, I saved it." Some locals are also working on the data center. Angel Crawford While some construction workers traveled to work on Meta's data center, others were locals leveraging the opportunity that arrived in their backyard, Angel said. "A lot of young men in this area work offshore at oil rigs, so it's a lot of time spent away from home," she said. "We know a lot of young people who are working at the construction site right now who would usually be off working away from home." She added, "Hopefully, it'll bring more jobs to the area for our kids and grandkids." There's uncertainty around how long construction workers will remain in Richland Parish. Angel Crawford Construction on Meta's data center is expected to continue for several years, but there's uncertainty among workers about how long they'll be in Richland Parish. "Most of them don't know how long they're going to be here. They hope they're going to be here long-term, but in construction, they don't get told until it's done," Angel said. Month-to-month leasing is among the top requests from tenants. A future without Meta. Business Insider Although Meta's presence in Richland Parish has become the new normal, it won't last forever. The data center will eventually become operational, meaning construction will wane, and workers will leave. The Crawfords have thought about a future without Meta, and they're not worried. "Each home in our mobile park is on one-fourth of an acre. After Meta's gone, we can sell them individually or rent them out," Angel said. For now, though, they're focused on the economic benefits that have come to Richland Parish from the data center project. "We've seen a lot of laundromats, RV parks, and mobile home parks come to the area," Angel said. "It's great for the economy in our area because people who we've worked with who install electrical systems, septic systems, plumbing, gravel, and all those things are busy because Meta's here." Angel said there are a few common requests among the construction and operational workers under Meta.

"As soon as they get into their rentals, 'What's the WiFi password?' is their first question," Angel said. "Some don't have their family here, so they want to do FaceTime."

The tenants also value an escape from the bustling construction site.

"They're with a lot of people all day long. They don't want to come home to a lot of noise," Angel said. "All of them say they love the peace and quiet."

Workforce housing is more popular than ever.

Angel Crawford

The demand for lodging in the area has continued to grow, Angel said.

"I get phone calls or text messages almost daily. Most of them are from my current tenants who have met someone who's looking for somewhere to stay," she said. "If you go on any of the websites, like Realtor.com, not all local rental properties are listed on there."

That's what led her to create StayNELA, a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners in 2025.

"I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. I kept a log, took pictures, and kept them in a folder on my phone. If anything was on Facebook about a rental, I saved it."

Some locals are also working on the data center.

Angel Crawford

While some construction workers traveled to work on Meta's data center, others were locals leveraging the opportunity that arrived in their backyard, Angel said.

"A lot of young men in this area work offshore at oil rigs, so it's a lot of time spent away from home," she said. "We know a lot of young people who are working at the construction site right now who would usually be off working away from home."

She added, "Hopefully, it'll bring more jobs to the area for our kids and grandkids."

There's uncertainty around how long construction workers will remain in Richland Parish.

Angel Crawford

Construction on Meta's data center is expected to continue for several years, but there's uncertainty among workers about how long they'll be in Richland Parish.

"Most of them don't know how long they're going to be here. They hope they're going to be here long-term, but in construction, they don't get told until it's done," Angel said.

Month-to-month leasing is among the top requests from tenants.

A future without Meta.

Business Insider

Although Meta's presence in Richland Parish has become the new normal, it won't last forever.

The data center will eventually become operational, meaning construction will wane, and workers will leave. The Crawfords have thought about a future without Meta, and they're not worried.

"Each home in our mobile park is on one-fourth of an acre. After Meta's gone, we can sell them individually or rent them out," Angel said.

For now, though, they're focused on the economic benefits that have come to Richland Parish from the data center project.

"We've seen a lot of laundromats, RV parks, and mobile home parks come to the area," Angel said. "It's great for the economy in our area because people who we've worked with who install electrical systems, septic systems, plumbing, gravel, and all those things are busy because Meta's here."
