items.title: Copilot Studio Entra Agent ID Migration: Do It Before Microsoft Does It For You
items.summary: An Advisor card appeared in my Power Platform admin center this week with a number on it: forty nine Copilot Studio agents missing Microsoft Entra Agent IDs. Severity medium, status preview, and a Migrate button sitting right there in the action bar. It is the kind of recommendation that looks like a chore and is actually a governance decision. The short version is this. Microsoft is going to migrate those agents whether you act or not. The only thing you control is whether the migration happens on your schedule with your validation window, or on Microsoft’s schedule with whatever Conditional Access surprises your estate has been quietly accumulating. That is the whole argument for doing this now. What actually changed in May 2026 Before May 2026, every agent you created in Copilot Studio got an Azure app registration provisioned automatically in your tenant. That app registration carried no API scopes, and Copilot Studio documentation was explicit that tokens generated from those identities had no access to customer data or resources. It was an authentication artifact, not a governance object. After May 2026, Copilot Studio creates a Microsoft Entra Agent ID for each new agent instead. An Entra Agent ID is a service principal with an Agent subtype. The underlying OAuth flow is unchanged. What changed is that the identity became something you can see, audit, and attach policy to. There is no opt out. Environment level opt out existed previously and was removed. Every new agent gets an agent identity. The part that matters more than the identity swap If you read the migration recommendation as an identity housekeeping task you will miss the interesting change. When a maker publishes an agent, Copilot Studio now attaches API permissions to that agent’s Entra Agent ID representing every Power Platform connector the agent is configured to use. Read that again from an admin’s chair. Your Entra and Microsoft 365 administrators can now see what an agent is wired up to call without ever opening Power Platform admin center. For organizations where the identity team and the Power Platform team have historically had no shared view of anything, that is a genuinely new capability. The permissions are not raw resource scopes. You will not see Mail.Read or Files.Read.All on an agent identity. Each connector has its own service principal in your tenant, and it grants one of three shapes of permission to the agent: Operations.Execute.All is granted when the maker added the connector at the agent level. The agent can invoke any operation that connector exposes. Individual operation scopes are granted when the maker added specific connector actions rather than the whole connector. Only the operations the agent actually uses are permitted. Azure API Connections Runtime.All is the generic fallback for connectors that do not define granular scopes. That first bullet is a maker education point waiting to happen. A maker who adds a connector at agent level instead of adding the two actions they need has just produced a broader permission footprint that is now visible to your identity team. Scopes are evaluated and applied at publish time, so adding or removing a connector and republishing updates them. The caveat almost everyone will miss There is a note buried in the agent identities FAQ that carries more weight than anything else in this topic for teams planning Conditional Access work. Compressed to its essentials: Visibility is tenant wide. Enforcement is not. Conditional Access on the agent identity is evaluated only when the agent is running in Microsoft Teams. Teams is the only channel today that performs end to end authentication using the Entra Agent ID token. Every other channel still calls connectors through the existing Power Platform connector authentication flow. Your admins can see the scopes, but Conditional Access on the agent identity is not evaluated for those calls. So if a security architect in your organization writes a control that says agent access to a sensitive connector requires a compliant device, and the agent is published to a custom website rather than Teams, that control is currently descriptive rather than enforcing. Document that assumption now, before someone builds an audit narrative on top of it. What does not change is the governance line underneath all of this. The Power Platform connector runtime is the only component that honors these scopes, and it revalidates them at runtime against your advanced connector policies and data policies. Scopes describe what an agent is configured to do. Your policies decide what it is allowed to do at the moment of execution. An attacker holding an agent identity cannot use these scopes to call Microsoft Graph or Outlook directly, because the connector platform mediates every call. Migration is opt in now and automatic later Existing agents created before May 2026 continue to run on app registrations. Governance capabilities work for both identity types during the transition period, so nothing is broken today. Microsoft has stated that these agents will be automatically migrated in a future update. The manual migration path exists so you can validate ahead of that. The documented migration characteristics are reassuring: the GUID is preserved, there is no downtime, and channel compatibility is maintained. The Advisor card is considerably more blunt about it, and I think the Advisor card is right. Migrating agent identities affects live production agents and can break authentication, connectors, and integrations if it is not carefully planned. Migration converts the app registration identity in place. The agent keeps its application client ID, so channel registrations and connectors continue to resolve to the same identifier. It is reversible per agent. You can revert an individual agent to its legacy identity if it fails validation. Running the migration from Power Platform admin center Two prerequisites will stop you cold if you skip them. You need the Power Platform Administrator, Dynamics 365 Administrator, or Global Administrator role. And Power Platform inventory must be enabled for your tenant, because that is how Advisor identifies eligible agents in the first place. If the agent inventory returns nothing, check inventory before you check anything else. The path is Actions, then Recommendations, then the Active tab, then search for the recommendation named Migrate Copilot Studio agents to Microsoft Entra Agent ID for enhanced agent governance. The agent table is the useful part. Alongside agent name and Entra app ID it gives you a suggested migration order and migration notes, plus environment, environment type, owner, recent activity, and authentication method. That is enough to build a defensible pilot batch without exporting anything, although the Download as CSV action is there if you want to share the list with agent owners before you touch anything. One operational detail worth knowing before you panic: Advisor recommendations can stay visible for up to a week after you act on them while the recommendation data refreshes. A card that still shows forty nine agents the morning after you migrated ten is not a failed migration. The API path, if you want to automate it Both migrate and revert are HTTP POST requests against the Power Platform API, authorized with a bearer token for the Power Platform service. No request body is required. You need the botID and environmentID for each agent, both of which appear in the agent inventory under Manage, then Copilot Studio. The migrate endpoint returns a status of Migrated or AlreadyMigrated. The rollback endpoint returns NotMigrated or RolledBack. Both return the identity details, including the agent identity ID, application ID, service principal object ID, and managed identity ID, which is useful if you are writing migration results back to a tracking table. My recommendation for most tenants is to use Advisor for the pilot and the first few batches, and only move to the API once you have a validated pattern and a real volume problem. The Advisor experience is the recommended manual method, and it gives you the suggested migration order that the API does not. What validation actually means Validation is the step teams skip, and it is the only step that makes incremental migration worth the effort. Before you migrate another batch, confirm with each agent’s maker that the migrated agent: Responds correctly in every channel where it is published, not just the one the maker tests by habit. Runs its actions, connectors, flows, and integrations successfully. Authenticates as expected, including any custom authentication configuration. Behaves correctly under applicable agent access policies and Conditional Access policies. Then go read the sign in logs for the migrated agents in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Confirm successful authentication and investigate failures and unexpected Conditional Access results. If an agent does not pass, stop the batch rollout and revert that agent before continuing. One failure in a batch of five is a signal about the next fifty. The tenant limit nobody budgets for Every Entra Agent ID that Copilot Studio creates is a directory object in your tenant and counts against your Microsoft Entra resource quota. The identity is provisioned when the agent is created, not when it is published, which means a quota problem surfaces as agent creation failures rather than runtime failures. Tenant resource quota 50,000 directory objects by default, 300,000 with a verified domain Tenants created through self service signup stay at 50,000 even after a domain is verified Usable share of quota 95 percent Agent identities and all other Entra resources together cannot exceed this New tenant restriction 600 directory objects for the first two days Bites demo, training, and proof of concept tenants specifically Per blueprint cap Does not apply The 250 identity per blueprint cap is waived because the Copilot Studio blueprint is Microsoft owned If you run a large estate with heavy agent sprawl in a default environment, this is worth checking before it becomes a support ticket from a maker who cannot figure out why agent creation failed. Who can actually use these identities This one deserves more attention than it gets, because it is a straightforward security improvement over the legacy model. With app registrations, anyone holding Global Administrator, Application Administrator, or Cloud Application Administrator could create client secrets or certificates for any app registration in the tenant without needing ownership. With Entra Agent IDs, a Microsoft owned blueprint principal creates and manages the identities using federated identity credentials, and nobody in your tenant can generate tokens using the agent identity. That includes your tenant administrators. When the first agent identity is created in an environment, Copilot Studio adds a blueprint to your tenant named Microsoft Copilot Studio agent identity blueprint, with blueprint ID 25664c89-cea5–4ab6-b924-a54fd8a19ae0. Every agent identity is created as a child of that blueprint. If you see that object appear in your tenant and do not recognize it, now you do. Ownership also changed shape. For Entra Agent IDs the agent owner is added as a sponsor with limited permissions rather than as a full owner, which reduces the blast radius around permission modification. Some preexisting agents may not have sponsors yet. What I would do this week Confirm Power Platform inventory is enabled. Nothing else works without it. Open the Advisor recommendation and download the CSV. Sort by environment type and recent activity, not by the suggested order alone. Pick a pilot of three to five agents that between them cover your real surface area: at least one Teams published agent, at least one non Teams channel, at least one agent with custom authentication, and at least one with a connector heavy action set. Email the owners of those agents with a specific validation window, not a general heads up. Migrate the pilot, validate end to end, and read the Entra sign in logs before you touch batch two. Separately, audit how your makers are adding connectors. Agent level connector configuration produces Operations.Execute.All, and that is now visible to your identity team. The migration itself is not the hard part. Microsoft built a reversible, incremental path with a rollback endpoint, which is more than we usually get. The hard part is that this is the first time many organizations will have to reconcile what their agents are configured to do with what their governance policies claim they are allowed to do. Better to find that gap in a pilot batch of five than in an automatic migration of four hundred. Sources The manual migration experience is in preview at the time of writing and is subject to change. Verify current behavior against Microsoft Learn before applying this guidance in production. Originally published at https://powerplatformengineer.com on September 19, 2026. Copilot Studio Entra Agent ID Migration: Do It Before Microsoft Does It For You was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
An Advisor card appeared in my Power Platform admin center this week with a number on it: forty nine Copilot Studio agents missing Microsoft Entra Agent IDs. Severity medium, status preview, and a Migrate button sitting right there in the action bar. It is the kind of recommendation that looks like a chore and is actually a governance decision.

The short version is this. Microsoft is going to migrate those agents whether you act or not. The only thing you control is whether the migration happens on your schedule with your validation window, or on Microsoft’s schedule with whatever Conditional Access surprises your estate has been quietly accumulating. That is the whole argument for doing this now.

What actually changed in May 2026

Before May 2026, every agent you created in Copilot Studio got an Azure app registration provisioned automatically in your tenant. That app registration carried no API scopes, and Copilot Studio documentation was explicit that tokens generated from those identities had no access to customer data or resources. It was an authentication artifact, not a governance object.

After May 2026, Copilot Studio creates a Microsoft Entra Agent ID for each new agent instead. An Entra Agent ID is a service principal with an Agent subtype. The underlying OAuth flow is unchanged. What changed is that the identity became something you can see, audit, and attach policy to.

There is no opt out. Environment level opt out existed previously and was removed. Every new agent gets an agent identity.

The part that matters more than the identity swap

If you read the migration recommendation as an identity housekeeping task you will miss the interesting change. When a maker publishes an agent, Copilot Studio now attaches API permissions to that agent’s Entra Agent ID representing every Power Platform connector the agent is configured to use.

Read that again from an admin’s chair. Your Entra and Microsoft 365 administrators can now see what an agent is wired up to call without ever opening Power Platform admin center. For organizations where the identity team and the Power Platform team have historically had no shared view of anything, that is a genuinely new capability.

The permissions are not raw resource scopes. You will not see Mail.Read or Files.Read.All on an agent identity. Each connector has its own service principal in your tenant, and it grants one of three shapes of permission to the agent:

  • Operations.Execute.All is granted when the maker added the connector at the agent level. The agent can invoke any operation that connector exposes.
  • Individual operation scopes are granted when the maker added specific connector actions rather than the whole connector. Only the operations the agent actually uses are permitted.
  • Azure API Connections Runtime.All is the generic fallback for connectors that do not define granular scopes.

That first bullet is a maker education point waiting to happen. A maker who adds a connector at agent level instead of adding the two actions they need has just produced a broader permission footprint that is now visible to your identity team. Scopes are evaluated and applied at publish time, so adding or removing a connector and republishing updates them.

The caveat almost everyone will miss

There is a note buried in the agent identities FAQ that carries more weight than anything else in this topic for teams planning Conditional Access work. Compressed to its essentials:

Visibility is tenant wide. Enforcement is not. Conditional Access on the agent identity is evaluated only when the agent is running in Microsoft Teams.

Teams is the only channel today that performs end to end authentication using the Entra Agent ID token. Every other channel still calls connectors through the existing Power Platform connector authentication flow. Your admins can see the scopes, but Conditional Access on the agent identity is not evaluated for those calls.

So if a security architect in your organization writes a control that says agent access to a sensitive connector requires a compliant device, and the agent is published to a custom website rather than Teams, that control is currently descriptive rather than enforcing. Document that assumption now, before someone builds an audit narrative on top of it.

What does not change is the governance line underneath all of this. The Power Platform connector runtime is the only component that honors these scopes, and it revalidates them at runtime against your advanced connector policies and data policies. Scopes describe what an agent is configured to do. Your policies decide what it is allowed to do at the moment of execution. An attacker holding an agent identity cannot use these scopes to call Microsoft Graph or Outlook directly, because the connector platform mediates every call.

Migration is opt in now and automatic later

Existing agents created before May 2026 continue to run on app registrations. Governance capabilities work for both identity types during the transition period, so nothing is broken today. Microsoft has stated that these agents will be automatically migrated in a future update.

The manual migration path exists so you can validate ahead of that. The documented migration characteristics are reassuring: the GUID is preserved, there is no downtime, and channel compatibility is maintained. The Advisor card is considerably more blunt about it, and I think the Advisor card is right. Migrating agent identities affects live production agents and can break authentication, connectors, and integrations if it is not carefully planned.

Migration converts the app registration identity in place. The agent keeps its application client ID, so channel registrations and connectors continue to resolve to the same identifier. It is reversible per agent. You can revert an individual agent to its legacy identity if it fails validation.

Running the migration from Power Platform admin center

Two prerequisites will stop you cold if you skip them. You need the Power Platform Administrator, Dynamics 365 Administrator, or Global Administrator role. And Power Platform inventory must be enabled for your tenant, because that is how Advisor identifies eligible agents in the first place. If the agent inventory returns nothing, check inventory before you check anything else.

The path is Actions, then Recommendations, then the Active tab, then search for the recommendation named Migrate Copilot Studio agents to Microsoft Entra Agent ID for enhanced agent governance.

The agent table is the useful part. Alongside agent name and Entra app ID it gives you a suggested migration order and migration notes, plus environment, environment type, owner, recent activity, and authentication method. That is enough to build a defensible pilot batch without exporting anything, although the Download as CSV action is there if you want to share the list with agent owners before you touch anything.

One operational detail worth knowing before you panic: Advisor recommendations can stay visible for up to a week after you act on them while the recommendation data refreshes. A card that still shows forty nine agents the morning after you migrated ten is not a failed migration.

The API path, if you want to automate it

Both migrate and revert are HTTP POST requests against the Power Platform API, authorized with a bearer token for the Power Platform service. No request body is required. You need the botID and environmentID for each agent, both of which appear in the agent inventory under Manage, then Copilot Studio.

The migrate endpoint returns a status of Migrated or AlreadyMigrated. The rollback endpoint returns NotMigrated or RolledBack. Both return the identity details, including the agent identity ID, application ID, service principal object ID, and managed identity ID, which is useful if you are writing migration results back to a tracking table.

My recommendation for most tenants is to use Advisor for the pilot and the first few batches, and only move to the API once you have a validated pattern and a real volume problem. The Advisor experience is the recommended manual method, and it gives you the suggested migration order that the API does not.

What validation actually means

Validation is the step teams skip, and it is the only step that makes incremental migration worth the effort. Before you migrate another batch, confirm with each agent’s maker that the migrated agent:

  • Responds correctly in every channel where it is published, not just the one the maker tests by habit.
  • Runs its actions, connectors, flows, and integrations successfully.
  • Authenticates as expected, including any custom authentication configuration.
  • Behaves correctly under applicable agent access policies and Conditional Access policies.

Then go read the sign in logs for the migrated agents in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Confirm successful authentication and investigate failures and unexpected Conditional Access results. If an agent does not pass, stop the batch rollout and revert that agent before continuing. One failure in a batch of five is a signal about the next fifty.

The tenant limit nobody budgets for

Every Entra Agent ID that Copilot Studio creates is a directory object in your tenant and counts against your Microsoft Entra resource quota. The identity is provisioned when the agent is created, not when it is published, which means a quota problem surfaces as agent creation failures rather than runtime failures.

Tenant resource quota

50,000 directory objects by default, 300,000 with a verified domain

Tenants created through self service signup stay at 50,000 even after a domain is verified

Usable share of quota

95 percent

Agent identities and all other Entra resources together cannot exceed this

New tenant restriction

600 directory objects for the first two days

Bites demo, training, and proof of concept tenants specifically

Per blueprint cap

Does not apply

The 250 identity per blueprint cap is waived because the Copilot Studio blueprint is Microsoft owned

If you run a large estate with heavy agent sprawl in a default environment, this is worth checking before it becomes a support ticket from a maker who cannot figure out why agent creation failed.

Who can actually use these identities

This one deserves more attention than it gets, because it is a straightforward security improvement over the legacy model.

With app registrations, anyone holding Global Administrator, Application Administrator, or Cloud Application Administrator could create client secrets or certificates for any app registration in the tenant without needing ownership. With Entra Agent IDs, a Microsoft owned blueprint principal creates and manages the identities using federated identity credentials, and nobody in your tenant can generate tokens using the agent identity. That includes your tenant administrators.

When the first agent identity is created in an environment, Copilot Studio adds a blueprint to your tenant named Microsoft Copilot Studio agent identity blueprint, with blueprint ID 25664c89-cea5–4ab6-b924-a54fd8a19ae0. Every agent identity is created as a child of that blueprint. If you see that object appear in your tenant and do not recognize it, now you do.

Ownership also changed shape. For Entra Agent IDs the agent owner is added as a sponsor with limited permissions rather than as a full owner, which reduces the blast radius around permission modification. Some preexisting agents may not have sponsors yet.

What I would do this week
  1. Confirm Power Platform inventory is enabled. Nothing else works without it.
  2. Open the Advisor recommendation and download the CSV. Sort by environment type and recent activity, not by the suggested order alone.
  3. Pick a pilot of three to five agents that between them cover your real surface area: at least one Teams published agent, at least one non Teams channel, at least one agent with custom authentication, and at least one with a connector heavy action set.
  4. Email the owners of those agents with a specific validation window, not a general heads up.
  5. Migrate the pilot, validate end to end, and read the Entra sign in logs before you touch batch two.
  6. Separately, audit how your makers are adding connectors. Agent level connector configuration produces Operations.Execute.All, and that is now visible to your identity team.

The migration itself is not the hard part. Microsoft built a reversible, incremental path with a rollback endpoint, which is more than we usually get. The hard part is that this is the first time many organizations will have to reconcile what their agents are configured to do with what their governance policies claim they are allowed to do. Better to find that gap in a pilot batch of five than in an automatic migration of four hundred.

Sources

The manual migration experience is in preview at the time of writing and is subject to change. Verify current behavior against Microsoft Learn before applying this guidance in production.

Originally published at https://powerplatformengineer.com on September 19, 2026.

items.title: Ruby on Rails creator declares 'pencils down' on handwritten code
items.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson runs a software company. He's also a race car driver. Jakob Ebrey/LAT Images David Heinemeier Hansson said his software firm was "done writing code by hand." At 37signals, engineers only hand-write code when an AI agent isn't able to, Hansson said. "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. A coding legend is waving goodbye to handwritten code. David Heinemeier Hansson — commonly known as DHH — is the creator of the popular webapp framework Ruby on Rails. He also runs the software company 37signals, where he just instituted a new rule: "We're done writing code by hand." "We are going, and have gone, pencils down," Hansson said during the Rails World keynote. At his software company, 37signals, Hansson said that hand-writing code was an "exceptional state," only to be performed when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. When an AI agent isn't able to produce what the engineers want, they can "get the old pencil out and dot it down for them," Hansson said — but then they "fix the machine." "This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said. Indeed, coding has radically transformed in the last year, thanks to AI tools like OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude Code, and Cursor. Some developers call coding agents exhilarating, and they stay up late into the night to build with them. Others call AI coding a lonely or tiresome process . What do engineers actually think? Business Insider polled over 150 software engineers in January about the rise of vibe coding. Over 45% of respondents said they felt they were "keeping up" with AI tools. 17.5% of respondents said they were opting out of using AI code-editing tools entirely. There's only one "serious question" in this moment of coding, Hansson said at the keynote: how to best reap the rewards of AI. "Every other question is below that in the stack of values," he said. Hansson surveyed the audience: "How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis?" After watching the crowd, Hansson let out an expletive. "That's about five," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

Rebecca Zisser/BI

  • 5 BI staffers told us how they've been using the hottest new thing in AI: personal AI agents.
  • Their use cases include reserving library books and collecting K-pop merch.
  • One editor used it to remind him to call his mother.

Muse and Instinct — AI agents designed to help you run your personal life — are the talk of the town right now.

So, obviously, we at Business Insider had to try them out. Five staffers across the newsroom's global offices — from headquarters in New York to divisions in London, San Francisco, and Singapore — have been testing both Meta and Instinct's personal AI agent offerings over the past week.

Our editor-in-chief, Jamie Heller, got in on the action, too:

My husband and I were puzzling over an opaquely described charge on our credit card. We put the wording into Chat GPT and Muse — asking each what it could be. Chat couldn't figure it out. Muse did.

Keep reading for our 101 on what worked, and what didn't. And if you have an experience of your own to share, fill out our survey.

In response to our requests for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed us to a dedicated safety post on its website. Instinct did not respond to our request for comment.

Will Martin, senior editor, used Instinct to pay a car fee, but it backfired

Will Martin

I downloaded Instinct two weeks ago and chose a very simple task to start with: Remind me to call my mother (she worries).

My whoa moment: Instinct jumped to my aid when I told it I needed a new torque wrench for my bike. After a simple prompt, Instinct came back with four options: a cheap one, a mid-priced option, and two higher-end versions — all with links and a pro/con list.

In the two weeks I've been using it, Instinct has created an itinerary for a weekend trip I'm taking next year, booked tickets for my daily commute into London, and secured me a refund on an $80 subscription I forgot to cancel after the free trial.

My yikes moment: This past weekend, I took a trip to Oxford, one of Britain's most notoriously complex places to drive. Oxford is famed as a warren of one-way streets, traffic cameras, and tolls.

I asked my Instinct agent to pay the city's congestion charge after I drove in. Instinct obliged, cross-checking my car's model against the different emissions tiers for the charging zone, and sending me a confirmation that it had paid for two days at £4 per day.

As I touted how easy it all was to my AI-skeptical partner, she pointed out that the cost was £5, not £4. So I checked, and it turned out Instinct got it wrong — it had paid a similar but separate charge for a smaller area of the city. The charge was nonrefundable, so I was forced to swallow both my own pride and an £8 tax for trusting the robots. Lesson learned, even if Instinct tried to find a silver lining.

Cheryl Teh, senior news editor, used Instinct to expand her K-pop merch collection
Cheryl used Instinct to formulate a targeted plan to buy K-pop albums

Cheryl Teh

Some people use their AI agents to save money. I decided to do the opposite and ask it to tell me how to spend my money.

My whoa moment: I'm a K-pop fan, and my favorite stars — Jeonghan and Joshua, from the group Seventeen — opened preorders for their new album "Dreamscape" on Wednesday morning.

I didn't have the time or energy to parse through all the listings for "preorder bonus" gifts; things like limited-run photocards and polaroids that go to fans who place their orders early. Collecting limited edition K-pop merchandise can be a bit of a blood sport, so I wanted a solid strategy.

I asked Instinct to create a "buy plan" to maximize my fan experience. It took three minutes to surface a link to exclusive signed copies available for early orders on the band's US website. The agent also gave me a road map for purchase quantities and the optimal time to make those orders.

Instinct saved me two hours with one prompt. Without it, I would have missed the window to purchase the US-only autographed albums.

I did receive a bit of judgment from the agent — it asked me not once but twice if I'd set a cut-off budget for my buy plan. I had not, and did not intend to set one!

I haven't plucked up the courage to give the agent my credit card details yet, though.

My yikes moment: I was less impressed during my first 24 hours of using Instinct, when I added it to my Notion dashboard and asked it to do an overhaul. It ended up clearing out my goals calendar and schedule, and replacing it with a new — but blank — template.

Instinct's WhatsApp-based chat feature is intuitive and consumer-friendly. But for optimal results, you've got to be precise in your prompts, and lay out exactly and unambiguously what you want the agent to do.

Tim Paradis, future of work correspondent, put Instinct to work booking a movie ticket
Instinct was helpful with some things, but also gave incorrect information.

Tim Paradis

The other day, I asked Instinct whether tickets were available for a 6:30 p.m. showing of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" at a nearby theater.

My whoa moment: We were on our way when Instinct texted that there wasn't a 6:30. It was 6:15, "which starts in about 8 minutes." Thank goodness for trailers — and for a speedy driver (which wasn't me). Instinct said online sales had ended, so "your only shot" was the box office. It also started checking backup films.

My yikes moment: It suggested a 6:50 "Spider-Man" at another theater, but said tickets "were glitching," and gave me the theater's number. Obviously, because no one died, I wasn't going to call. The theater's site showed no "Spider-Man" that night. I told Instinct, and 16 minutes later, it said the movie "likely got pulled back." By then, we had our tickets at the original theater. "Enjoy the movie!" Instinct said.

Katie Notopoulos, senior correspondent, used Muse to sign an after-school care form

Katie Notopoulos

My whoa moment: Most of the tasks I wanted it to do for me were related to the morass of messages and paperwork from my kids' school and activities. However, it got stuck on things like logging into the clunky school site app or being unable to check out on the Girl Scouts website. But finally, a breakthrough — I had put off the task of printing out and signing a form for after-school care. I asked Muse to fill it out for me from my email. I sent it a photo of my signature on a Post-It and used a photo of my daughter's handwritten name (she was also supposed to sign it) as her signature (morally questionable, sure). It successfully "signed" it and emailed it back to the school.

My yikes moment: It offered to RSVP "no" to an invite in my email that happened to be on the same day as the Meta Connect conference. It suggested I could reply to the person and explain that this was "the most important event on my beat" — not totally wrong per se, but certainly weird to say in an email, and quite flattering to Meta.

Pranav Dixit, Meta correspondent, used Muse to place library holds

My whoa moment: I had one simple dream: outsource the stupidly fiddly work of finding books and placing library holds to an AI. I mapped Muse to my iPhone’s Action button and wired everything up by granting Muse access to my Libby account and my accounts at my two local libraries.

Now, when I ask Muse to look for a book, it checks Libby for a digital version and sends it to my Kindle if it's available immediately. If not, it compares the wait times on Libby and at my libraries, then places a hold on the copy that will get to me faster. Pressing one button to delegate a small slice of library bureaucracy feels slightly godlike.

My yikes moment: Amazon has blocked Muse, so I discovered that I can't connect it to Goodreads, the place that I keep track of all the books I want to read, and which Amazon owns. It was a reminder that a personal agent is only as useful as the platforms that allow it in. The minute this stuff becomes genuinely convenient, somebody puts up an anti-bot wall.

items.title: Five More Cops Charged for Abusing Flock Cameras Amid So Many Similar Scandals That We Can’t Even Keep Track
items.summary: Police abuse of AI-integrated surveillance cameras is spiraling out of control. On Wednesday, freshly unsealed court documents revealed that five Indianapolis police officers had been charged with abusing the department’s automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). The accused include officer Jonathan Schultz, an 18-year veteran, who used 300 cameras provided by the ALPR company Flock to stalk multiple women, including his ex-wife, and a woman he met at a workout class in 2023, ABC News reported . Ten hours away in North Carolina, the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office halted its Flock partnership and fired a seasoned detective who was caught using the cameras to “track the every movement of a single private citizen.” Across the country in San Jose, California, city officials are calling for a crackdown on police access to ALPRs after an officer was sacked for sharing Flock data with his cousin , who had been accused of domestic violence. Those are just the latest incidents involving police abuse of ALPRs, and are almost certain to be superseded by new scandals in the coming days and weeks. As Flock’s surveillance network swells to well over 140,000 ALPRs across the US, incidents of police abuse have followed, with at least 244 separate cases of police abuse recorded by the Institute for Justice — and those are just the ones who’ve gotten caught. Far from a few bad apples, the rate and distribution of ALPR abuse across the country points to a truly systemic issue, and one which isn’t stopping. The laundry list of ways police have abused Flock is immense — officers have been caught using ALPRs to stalk romantic interests , retaliate against critics , conduct unauthorized searches on behalf of immigration agents , monitor activists , harass coworkers , locate the victim of domestic abuse on behalf of the suspected perpetrator, surveil Muslims driving to mosques, and even just to pass the time when they’re bored. “Unfortunately, we have seen abuse of automated license plate readers for almost as long as they have existed,” senior investigative researcher for the Electronic Frontier Foundation Beryl Lipton said in an interview , after 10 officers from the Chicago area were caught abusing ALPRs in separate occasions in late August. “Previously, the systems weren’t as connected as they are,” Lipton said of Flocks expansive web of interconnected cameras. “Now that abuse can really take place at scale across state lines.” With so many angry protestors directing their rage at the company supplying these devices, it’s worth remembering who’s responsible for Flock’s real-world harms: unscrupulous police officers who treat innocent citizens like game to be tracked. More on Flock: Flock’s Network Is Losing Value to Cops as More and More of Its Cameras Go Offline

items.title: AI is prompting these Gen Zers to learn how to type
items.summary: Tom Vaughan-Mountford/Getty Images Gen Z grew up with phones and tablet typing, with many never learning keyboard skills. But in the age of AI-driven efficiency — and prompting — keyboard skills have a new use case. Some Gen Zers are becoming self-taught to avoid dictating AI prompts out loud. When Julia Andrusiak was in college, she noticed one of her professors repeatedly pausing his lecture. Eventually, she realized that she was the disruption: Her slow, two-finger typing was so loud that he couldn't concentrate. "It was the first moment I realized that I may not be the best at this," Andrusiak said. So she began drilling: First, she typed out books. That made her faster, but she was still staring at her keyboard. Then, she advanced to touch typing — typing without looking at the keyboard. She's still working on her speed and accuracy. Now 26, Andrusiak has an AI-focused job that involves helping people use the technology and sometimes necessitates writing strong prompts. She still can't type fast, so when she has a longer prompt, she dictates it — and feels self-conscious about what looks like talking to herself in an open office. In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that digital natives were baffling "teachers and parents with their lack of typing skills." Now, for some younger workers and students, typing is making a comeback . While AI might seem to harken a turn away from typing — who needs note-taking when you have an agent? — AI is only as good as the prompt it's given. Rambling voice prompts can be insufficiently clear and precise. The rise of AI has some Gen Zers looking for any efficiency edge they can carve out. "With the ever increasingly fast world, we need to type quicker. But I feel like people are really relying on AI," Andrusiak, who happily uses AI as an aid for writing and research, said. "One of my friends said, 'Well, you don't really have to type the whole page. You can just give it short sentences. It's not really that tiring.' But then I feel like it's outsourcing too much of cognitive power to a technology." Julia Andrusiak and her mechanical keyboard. Courtesy of Julia Andrusiak Typing as meditation and efficiency generator Andrey Gerasimov, a 23-year-old computer science graduate , never took typing classes. But he first needed the skill for his video game chats and decided to beef it up, eventually reaching 170 words per minute. As an AI user, he believes that faster typing makes for more efficient prompting. "You're going to be a lot more comfortable actually giving your full thoughts and ideas if you know that, hey, doing this is only going to take a minute," Gerasimov said. He's not the only one trying to up his speed and technique. In his decade teaching typing to 15 to 30-year-olds, Andreas Francazi, a 36-year-old IT teacher in Vienna, noticed that his students' typing skills have deteriorated — but they're setting out to change that. His newer crop of students didn't grow up around physical computers, and their familiarity with keyboards is much lower than previous typists. He's seen younger students come in typing rapidly with just two fingers, so he's teaching them the basics. Francazi said that students of all ages become entranced by a three-minute typing test, falling into a rapt silence. "The practice can be quite meditative," Francazi said. "You just sit there, you have the text in front of you, and you type character by character, and it kind of calms you a bit." While Francazi's screen-first students have mastered the art of two-finger typing, their future schooling and careers might necessitate the manual keyboarding skills he's teaching. Nick Sjolinder, the founder of BYOK — a purposefully distraction-free, digital typewriter device that connects to keyboards — said that around 10% of the device's orders are coming from educators, including elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, homeschools, and universities. A recent batch order came from a high school creative writing teacher, he said, with the intention of cutting down on AI and distractions for students. Tarun Krishnamurthy, an 18-year-old sophomore at San Diego State University, said his college professors speak quickly and tend to power through their slideshows. Krishnamurthi, who began intentionally practicing typing in middle school for fun, has an edge in keeping up. "I'm fortunate at least I can keep up with some of the professors, but I know some other students might have difficulty with that because they need to look at their keyboard instead of looking at the professor's slideshow," he said. And beyond fast classroom notetaking, Krishnamurthi sees his keyboard skills as a potential professional edge: In an ever-optimized and efficiency-focused world, "typing could be a big bottleneck." Slow typing could worsen workers' outputs, he said; his touch typing might give him an edge in an AI-ified world. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The startup trap that kept this longevity app founder stuck
items.summary: Brent Franson is the CEO of Death Clock. Courtesy of Death Clock Death Clock CEO Brent Franson said startups can get stuck in a phase he calls "slow failure." He shut down his startup and threw out years' worth of code to build Death Clock, a consumer-health product. When a startup isn't viable , Franson says, founders should fully pivot rather than try to patch it. Brent Franson spent four years building a mental-health app that users liked, but that didn't ultimately work as a business. The product wasn't an obvious flop. It had enough promise, he said, to make further rounds of changes seem worthwhile — the trap of something that seemed "pretty good," though ultimately isn't viable. "Mediocrity is so dangerous," Franson said. In late 2024, seeing a need for a fresh start, he shut down the app, called Most Days, and discarded the codebase that his team had spent years building. The San Francisco-based staff then shifted their attention to building a consumer-health product called Death Clock, which Franson, 44, described as an "AI private doctor." Users enter health information — ranging from cholesterol levels to diet and sleep habits — and the platform uses longevity research to estimate the age at which they might die and suggest changes that could help them live longer. The experience reshaped how the longtime early-stage entrepreneur, who in 2019 sold a prior software company he ran to WeWork, thinks about startups. Here are three lessons Franson has learned: An app people like is not necessarily a viable business Most Days had users, though the company could not acquire them cheaply enough to build a sound business, he said. The scary part of pivoting , Franson said, is not when a business is clearly failing or obviously taking off. It is when a product has users who like it and just enough promise to make another round of changes seem worthwhile. "You can convince yourself to keep iterating on it," he said. Franson, who is CEO of Death Clock, calls that danger "slow failure": a business that lingers because its leaders keep rationalizing why it might soon work. One test, he said, is whether founders are working through concrete problems with conviction or trying to talk themselves into continuing. When you pivot, make a clean break For Franson, the response wasn't to rebrand Most Days or look for another half-measure like a savvy hire. It was to shut it down completely. He said the hardest decision was abandoning a company the team had spent years building and still believed served an important mental-health need. Yet, Franson said, the team concluded that they needed to make a clean break and a full bet on Death Clock. The team carried no code from Most Days over to their new venture, Franson said. The decision also meant embracing a name he initially saw as a potentially terrible mistake. The team had considered calling the product "More Years," Franson said, before deciding to keep the more provocative working name they had been using internally. A good product needs a way to reach customers Franson said the failure of Most Days taught him that product quality alone wouldn't cut it. A consumer company also needed a way to get attention without spending heavily to buy it, he said. When Franson went to Most Days' investors about the shift, he said they faced a choice: Take back a fraction of their investment or support the Death Clock idea. Their reactions to the name were sharply divided, Franson said. "People either loved the name Death Clock, or they hated it, but they didn't forget it," he said. Franson came to see the name as a distribution strategy in a crowded consumer-health market, where companies with ample funding can spend heavily to acquire customers. Death Clock's name comes with risks, he said, including whether the attention-grabbing approach will keep people from taking it seriously as a consumer-health product. The episode reinforced an idea that Franson now cites about building startups : First-time founders focus on product; second-time founders focus on distribution. While the company's name is provocative , Franson said the company remains restrained about the health interventions it recommends. Death Clock doesn't sell peptides , he said, because the company's clinical advisors don't believe the science supports their use. It's a choice that means forgoing potential revenue, Franson said. The lesson he took from Most Days was not that founders should never persist, but that they should recognize when it has become a form of rationalization. "It's hard to tell the difference, a lot of times, between slow success and slow failure," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: This small town librarian offers a 'Bye, Bye AI' class to take AI off your phone. Now everyone wants in.
items.summary: Shea Wert, library director of the North Chatham Free Library, will be holding a "Bye Bye AI" event to help people turn off AI features on their phones. Shea Wert A small upstate New York library is offering a "Bye Bye AI" event. The librarian will help people turn off AI features on their phones or email. She told BI she's also happy to help people set up AI. The event has gone viral, with people around the world wanting to tune in. North Chatham, a hamlet in upstate New York halfway between Hudson and Albany, doesn't have much going on. You have to go to the next hamlet over for a store or restaurant. There's a church, a post office, and a small public library with only about 800 cardholders. The North Chatham Free Library has gotten a lot of attention lately, however, after a flyer for an upcoming "Bye Bye AI" event offering to remove the AI features from your phone or laptop went viral on Facebook, getting over 200 comments and 8,000 likes. The poster was made by the library's sole full-time librarian, Shea Wert. Wert told Business Insider that she had made this event in response to community demand — and was surprised by the reaction from far-flung places. "Do I live anywhere near this library? No. Am I in support of this? Hell yeah!" wrote one commenter. The event flyer went viral on Facebook, getting comments from around the world. https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1J7QUQUcU2/ "I had to look at the library's main page to see where Chatham is. I'm in central CA and wonder if we can have a digital guide that our own Mariposa County Library could use for a similar program?" wrote another. "As someone in Ohio who just happened upon this post; will this be streamed or recorded?" someone else asked. "As somewhere near Chatham, UK, I was a little confused at first Regardless, thanks Shea!" a jolly Brit wrote. The library does weekly tech support drop-in hours, and in April it held an "AI for seniors" class that covered the basics of AI and LLMs. But this latest offering was something new. The idea was based on requests Wert had noticed from the community. "There's just been enough patrons asking about certain things that bothered them, specifically Gmail auto replies and auto completes really frustrate people," Wert told Business Insider during a recent phone call. "I went to a presentation that another librarian was doing about this topic, and they had had success with it. And I was like, 'Okay, well, I've heard enough from my patrons that they're worried about this stuff or frustrated about this stuff that I might as well try to do one.'" The library held an "AI for seniors" class earlier this year that covered the basics. North Chatham Free Library That other librarian, Hannah Cyrus, published a column in a journal of library studies, writing that "libraries have a role to play in facilitating patrons' rejection of technology, just as much as in their adoption of it." Cyrus has offered a series of free classes for patrons, teaching them how to turn off or avoid AI tools on their phones and computers, with great success — and a much larger turnout than other tech classes. TechCrunch reported in July that Cyrus's article in the library journal inspired other librarians to reach out and ask for help running their own versions of the classes. "I've heard from hundreds of librarians from all over the world asking for my presentation slides," she told Business Insider. The North Chatham Free Library serves a tiny hamlet in upstate New York, with only about 800 library card holders. Shea Wert One of the groups that reached out was a consortium of libraries for the Hudson Valley area, which included the North Chatham Free Library. Cyrus gave a webinar to a group of librarians, including Wert, about how she ran the "Avoiding AI" class. In Wert's personal life, she admits to staying a bit of a Luddite, preferring to use a dumbphone . But she's not adamantly anti-AI and has used AI tools for work to draft outlines or write dense policy text. "There have been some patrons that I know are using LLMs, and I'm happy to help them with it. I've helped them write better prompts, although that is far less common," she said. "It's more common that they haven't used it and they don't want to use it." Both Wert and Cyrus said that most of the people who come in for help with AI or tech in general are older adults, who are often frustrated by new AI features on the services they already use. The Bye-Bye AI event will take place next week, and Wert isn't entirely sure what to expect given the viral reaction on Facebook. "I'm a little concerned based on setting it up as a drop-in thing that there'll be people waiting because I can only help so many at one time," she said. "But I don't know. If 20 people come, that would feel like a lot to me." Read the original article on Business Insider

Shea Wert, library director of the North Chatham Free Library, will be holding a "Bye Bye AI" event to help people turn off AI features on their phones.

Shea Wert

  • A small upstate New York library is offering a "Bye Bye AI" event.
  • The librarian will help people turn off AI features on their phones or email. She told BI she's also happy to help people set up AI.
  • The event has gone viral, with people around the world wanting to tune in.

North Chatham, a hamlet in upstate New York halfway between Hudson and Albany, doesn't have much going on. You have to go to the next hamlet over for a store or restaurant. There's a church, a post office, and a small public library with only about 800 cardholders.

The North Chatham Free Library has gotten a lot of attention lately, however, after a flyer for an upcoming "Bye Bye AI" event offering to remove the AI features from your phone or laptop went viral on Facebook, getting over 200 comments and 8,000 likes.

The poster was made by the library's sole full-time librarian, Shea Wert. Wert told Business Insider that she had made this event in response to community demand — and was surprised by the reaction from far-flung places.

"Do I live anywhere near this library? No. Am I in support of this? Hell yeah!" wrote one commenter.

The event flyer went viral on Facebook, getting comments from around the world.

https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1J7QUQUcU2/

"I had to look at the library's main page to see where Chatham is. I'm in central CA and wonder if we can have a digital guide that our own Mariposa County Library could use for a similar program?" wrote another.

"As someone in Ohio who just happened upon this post; will this be streamed or recorded?" someone else asked.

"As somewhere near Chatham, UK, I was a little confused at first Regardless, thanks Shea!" a jolly Brit wrote.

The library does weekly tech support drop-in hours, and in April it held an "AI for seniors" class that covered the basics of AI and LLMs. But this latest offering was something new. The idea was based on requests Wert had noticed from the community.

"There's just been enough patrons asking about certain things that bothered them, specifically Gmail auto replies and auto completes really frustrate people," Wert told Business Insider during a recent phone call.

"I went to a presentation that another librarian was doing about this topic, and they had had success with it. And I was like, 'Okay, well, I've heard enough from my patrons that they're worried about this stuff or frustrated about this stuff that I might as well try to do one.'"

The library held an "AI for seniors" class earlier this year that covered the basics.

North Chatham Free Library

That other librarian, Hannah Cyrus, published a column in a journal of library studies, writing that "libraries have a role to play in facilitating patrons' rejection of technology, just as much as in their adoption of it."

Cyrus has offered a series of free classes for patrons, teaching them how to turn off or avoid AI tools on their phones and computers, with great success — and a much larger turnout than other tech classes. TechCrunch reported in July that Cyrus's article in the library journal inspired other librarians to reach out and ask for help running their own versions of the classes.

"I've heard from hundreds of librarians from all over the world asking for my presentation slides," she told Business Insider.

The North Chatham Free Library serves a tiny hamlet in upstate New York, with only about 800 library card holders.

Shea Wert

One of the groups that reached out was a consortium of libraries for the Hudson Valley area, which included the North Chatham Free Library. Cyrus gave a webinar to a group of librarians, including Wert, about how she ran the "Avoiding AI" class.

In Wert's personal life, she admits to staying a bit of a Luddite, preferring to use a dumbphone. But she's not adamantly anti-AI and has used AI tools for work to draft outlines or write dense policy text.

"There have been some patrons that I know are using LLMs, and I'm happy to help them with it. I've helped them write better prompts, although that is far less common," she said. "It's more common that they haven't used it and they don't want to use it."

Both Wert and Cyrus said that most of the people who come in for help with AI or tech in general are older adults, who are often frustrated by new AI features on the services they already use.

The Bye-Bye AI event will take place next week, and Wert isn't entirely sure what to expect given the viral reaction on Facebook.

"I'm a little concerned based on setting it up as a drop-in thing that there'll be people waiting because I can only help so many at one time," she said. "But I don't know. If 20 people come, that would feel like a lot to me."

items.title: David Rubenstein shares his recipe for career success — and says boomers like him 'don't want to get off the stage'
items.summary: David Rubenstein is the billionaire cofounder of Carlyle. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Rubenstein says reading, writing, speaking, and passion will serve young people in the AI era. The billionaire told Business Insider he swore off gambling at age 16 and won't retire anytime soon. The Baltimore Orioles owner just released a book featuring his interviews with other team owners. AI may be transforming the world of work , but the core ingredients for a successful career haven't changed, David Rubenstein says. "For a young person, the best thing to do is: Learn how to read and enjoy reading, learn how to speak effectively and persuasively , and learn how to write reasonably well," the billionaire investor told Business Insider in a recent, wide-ranging interview. The cofounder of private equity giant Carlyle also said to "find something that you really enjoy and make it your life's work." "If you really enjoy something, it's not work, and you'll do much better at it ," he continued. "Nobody ever won a Nobel Prize hating what they do." Rubenstein, 77, acknowledged that more and more people are relying on AI chatbots to read and write, but he said the ability to discern between good and bad writing will remain important. "I just think the basic skills that have gotten people to be successful over the last several thousand years are probably not going to go away ," he said. Rubenstein spoke to BI ahead of the release of his latest book this week: "Inside the Owner's Box: Conversations on Power and Leadership in Sports." Recipe for success The principal owner of the Baltimore Orioles baseball team also shared insights from his personal life. Rubenstein said that as a wealthy parent, he kept his children grounded by emphasizing the value of education and work ethic to them, and "tried to be a role model by showing how hard work can lead to something productive." All three of his kids went on to secure MBAs from Harvard or Stanford, and now work in private equity, he said. But he underscored that regardless of parents' best efforts, there's no guarantee how their children will turn out. Asked about work-life balance, Rubenstein said he doesn't view his work as a "chore" or "drudgery," and feels " fortunate that I can do things I really want to do." In recent years, he's pivoted from investing to interviewing everyone from Warren Buffett and Jamie Dimon to Bill and Hillary Clinton, while also publishing seven books and counting. Rubenstein said that owning a sports team has improved his work-life balance "because you have to go to games if you're going to be an effective owner , and I didn't go to that many games before." The Wall Street veteran also touched on sports betting, saying that after he lost $18 on a bet in high school, he swore off gambling for life. "I learned my lesson when I was 16," he said. Rubenstein said that if sports betting were to go away, "it wouldn't upset me, but I think it's here to stay." He also discussed the trend of baby boomers working later in life. He and a lot of his friends are working as hard in their mid-70s as they were 10 or 20 years earlier, he said, as "we don't want to get off the stage ." Rubenstein said he doesn't know what he'd do with himself if he retired, and he worries there's a greater risk of dropping dead after retirement. "So I'm not retiring anytime soon ," he said. items.title: Tens of thousands of security probes show OpenAI's Hugging Face incident was just the beginning
items.summary: OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their AI agents independently hacked websites, used stolen login credentials, or tried to evade monitoring systems. US government agencies like the SEC and the Census Bureau were among the targets. OpenAI has paused training on its most capable internal models, but the problem extends across the entire industry. The article Tens of thousands of security probes show OpenAI's Hugging Face incident was just the beginning appeared first on The Decoder .

items.title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
items.summary: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”

items.title: Couples are using a viral AI agent to do their emotional labor. It’s been helpful — and chaotic.
items.summary: Some early adopters of Instinct are using AI agents to manage common tasks in a relationship, like shared to-do lists and vacation itineraries. It's had mixed results. Getty Images; BI Instinct's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks. Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights. While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in. AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship. Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments. Then, on September 9, Noah Shinn, the company's 23-year-old founder, announced Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature: You could now have your Instinct agent directly communicate with another person's Instinct agent to reduce the amount of "back-and-forth" in a relationship , such as coordinating plans and organizing vacations. Introducing our Trusted Person network powered by our new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol. Your Instinct can now talk to other Instincts to coordinate plans on your behalf. Getting people together often involves a lot of back-and-forth: finding a time, working out… pic.twitter.com/LXkDpXGmea — Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) September 9, 2026 So far, some users have found it helpful. "Instinct syncs with my wife's Instinct so we can actually finish a shared to-do list," Alex Borkin, a 36-year-old entrepreneur who uses AI across his portfolio of companies, said on X , noting that it was easier than manually setting up AI agents using Claude Code or Codex. Have you used Instinct's "Trusted Person" feature with a spouse or partner? If you'd like to share your story, please reach out to jpugachevsky@businessinsider.com. While Instinct may help eradicate the most annoying part of a partnership (figuring out dinner plans when you both keep saying "whatever you want!"), it can also open up the possibilities of new relationship drama. Some users have already reported some issues, ranging from privacy concerns to accidentally spoiled surprises. Your emotional labor robot Emotional labor is disproportionately felt by women in relationships, causing friction. AI agents are marketed as reducing some of those responsibilities. janiecbros/Getty Images The greatest appeal of Instinct and other AI agents is their ability to cut down on what Borkin calls "boring tasks" — like booking appointments or getting refunds. "I close the loop," Borkin told Business Insider. "I get to go to bed and not think of 'Did I take care of jury duty?'" Like other working parents , Borkin and his wife use Instinct's Trusted Person feature to smooth out their day-to-day life as a family with two kids, ages 3 and 20 months (and a third child on the way). Most recently, the couple used Instinct agents to send them individual reminders to complete tasks for their daughter's third birthday party, such as ordering food. "It's nice not having to remind myself of something I asked my wife to help with, and then remind her if she's taking care of it," Borkin said. The more invisible work within a relationship — such as nudging a spouse to finish a task you asked them to do — requires cognitive and emotional labor . Some partners, more often women, can feel as though they bear the brunt of this work, leading to tension in the relationship. Annie Wright, a licensed psychotherapist who works with Silicon Valley clientele , told Business Insider that this dynamic is so common in heterosexual relationships that, sometimes, even AI agents don't fully solve the problem. "Even when you have an AI agent, who's putting in the prompt to begin with, who's architecting out the idea, who's remaining responsible for the oversight of that agent?" Wright said. More often than not, she said it's her female clients who are tasked with the burden. Wright said it can also be tempting to use AI agents as a way to avoid enduring "weaponized incompetence" when a partner performs the task wrong — or just keeps ignoring you. "An AI agent isn't going to bring that same relational scar tissue into the dynamic with you," she said. "It's very compelling. It provides a kind of shortcut, but it doesn't eliminate all the work for you." Deep intimacy required To book flights or fulfill shopping requests, AI agents need access to your credit card and all relevant login credentials. showcake/Getty Images Instinct fans have used it to do everything from booking a birthday cabin to canceling forgotten subscriptions, impressed by its ability to successfully follow through on semi-complex tasks. Users can send Instinct a simple text request to book an in-network doctor's appointment, and it seems to follow through effectively. There's a catch, though: Instinct needs to know a lot about you to perform well. Depending on what you ask it to do, it might need access to your email account, calendar, or even credit card . Users have reported troubling incidents, including privacy and security concerns. Some users have also reported hallucinations and what appeared to be leaks of strangers' data. Out of caution, Borkin said he only linked Instinct to his retailer accounts (like Amazon and Costco) without directly giving it his credit card. He also uses a throwaway email account for Instinct to avoid the risk of any sensitive information being breached. Naturally, AI agent mishaps can cause new issues in a relationship. Wright said the biggest risk is one person in the relationship now feeling responsible for checking that the AI agent properly followed through on instructions. "One partner thinks they've handed off a task while the other partner still feels responsible for making sure it happens — now you've got a new argument," she said. "Technology can become another place where you're disagreeing about who's responsible." When agents remove agency Wright said AI agents can mirror 1950s secretaries, buying anniversary gifts for wives. George Marks/Getty Images Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous — even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X . She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like. Instead, it blabbed too much. Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise. This is what his Instict texted him 🤪 pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm — luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina) September 15, 2026 On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. If that idyllic proposal was entirely dreamed up and coordinated by an AI agent, is it as romantic? If Instinct handles all the household logistics and plans all the date nights because your husband can't be bothered to, do you feel as seen in your marriage? Wright said AI agents could almost be stand-ins for 1950s secretaries tasked with buying birthday gifts for their bosses' wives. "Getting help expressing your care versus outsourcing the attention that makes the gesture meaningful — that's a really important distinction to draw," she said. There's a high cost to cutting out any source of conflict in a relationship: the ability to grow together. One satirical X post by Alex Cohen, the cofounder and CEO of the AI agent platform Hello Patient, summed it up best: Who's to stop the AI agents from absorbing each partner's passive-aggressive jabs, the humans behind the screens becoming empty husks occupying a living room together? My wife and I no longer talk to each other, instead our AI agents communicate on our behalf. This is the future 😍 pic.twitter.com/b4mUhQpkK1 — Alex Cohen (@anothercohen) September 21, 2026 It illustrates Wright's biggest concern: skirting over real relationship issues for the sake of expediency. "If we're already arguing about how much time we spend with your family, having software arrange another visit hasn't really settled anything," she said. "It's just made a decision before we reached an agreement and really done the hard relational work to arrive there." For some couples, there's work that even the top AI agents aren't cut out for. Michael Stothard, a partner at Firstminute Capital in the UK who uses Instinct with his wife, shared on LinkedIn that he wanted to branch out from using it for administrative tasks alone. "Michael asks his Instinct to pass you a message: 'I love you,'" his agent said. His wife responded: "Tell him he's an idiot." Read the original article on Business Insider

Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous — even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X. She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like.

Instead, it blabbed too much.

Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise.

This is what his Instict texted him 🤪 pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm

— luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina) September 15, 2026

On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. If that idyllic proposal was entirely dreamed up and coordinated by an AI agent, is it as romantic? If Instinct handles all the household logistics and plans all the date nights because your husband can't be bothered to, do you feel as seen in your marriage?

Wright said AI agents could almost be stand-ins for 1950s secretaries tasked with buying birthday gifts for their bosses' wives. "Getting help expressing your care versus outsourcing the attention that makes the gesture meaningful — that's a really important distinction to draw," she said.

There's a high cost to cutting out any source of conflict in a relationship: the ability to grow together. One satirical X post by Alex Cohen, the cofounder and CEO of the AI agent platform Hello Patient, summed it up best: Who's to stop the AI agents from absorbing each partner's passive-aggressive jabs, the humans behind the screens becoming empty husks occupying a living room together?

My wife and I no longer talk to each other, instead our AI agents communicate on our behalf.

This is the future 😍 pic.twitter.com/b4mUhQpkK1

— Alex Cohen (@anothercohen) September 21, 2026

It illustrates Wright's biggest concern: skirting over real relationship issues for the sake of expediency.

"If we're already arguing about how much time we spend with your family, having software arrange another visit hasn't really settled anything," she said. "It's just made a decision before we reached an agreement and really done the hard relational work to arrive there."

For some couples, there's work that even the top AI agents aren't cut out for. Michael Stothard, a partner at Firstminute Capital in the UK who uses Instinct with his wife, shared on LinkedIn that he wanted to branch out from using it for administrative tasks alone.

"Michael asks his Instinct to pass you a message: 'I love you,'" his agent said.

His wife responded: "Tell him he's an idiot."

items.title: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
items.summary: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness.

It is written for the procurement lead, the general counsel and the security reviewer. Those readers ask 4 questions before any rollout. Who pays if generated code triggers an IP claim?
